title: Florida couple allegedly held four children in tractor-trailer cab for nearly seven years
description: Four children were allegedly confined in a tractor-trailer cab for nearly seven years without school, showers or medical care in a Florida neglect case.
fullText:
A Florida couple is being charged with child neglect after allegedly keeping four children confined in the cab of a tractor-trailer for almost seven years without "time to take showers, use the restroom" or "exercise outside," arrest records show.

The children "have not been allowed to attend school for approximately five years," they told interviewers at a child advocacy center, according to an arrest report.

Keisha Epps, 51, and her fiancé, Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, have been living in the cab with the children while Epps works as a truck driver, driving a route between Miami and Atlanta, according to court documents.

Since December 2019, the children were kept inside the vehicle "for the majority of their days."

Polygamous Sect Leader Convicted On State Charges After Girls Found In Unventilated Trailer

A detective on the case reported the children were "walking with an unnatural gait from being confined to the cab."

They were "fed poorly," and they never received medical or dental care—even for emergencies, the report shows.

During the interview, one of the children recalled a time she "burned herself badly with cooked noodles."

"There was a lot of blood," she said.

Neither Stewart nor Epps took her to get medical treatment, the child told investigators. The child has a "permanent scar" from the burn, court records show.

16 Children Found Living In 'Deplorable' Ohio Home Conditions, 4 Arrested: 'Pure Evil'

Stewart "would watch" the children when Epps was sleeping, showering and driving the truck, the children said. And when the children witnessed sexual abuse and confronted Stewart, he "beat them by punching them in their heads," reports show. The identity of the alleged victim of sexual abuse wasn't clear.

The children said they told Epps about the sexual abuse and saw her witness the sexual abuse. She called one "derogatory names and continued to leave them alone with" Stewart, reports show.

One of the children was found to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection.

All four children shared a bunk in the cab so small that they had to lie "curled up side by side because they could not fit," reports show.

Actor Charged With 24 Felony Counts In Alleged Child Sexual Abuse Case

Both Epps and Stewart were arrested on Aug. 6, 2026, according to a heavily redacted report filed with the court by the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office.

Epps and Stewart both were charged with four counts of child neglect—one count for each child. Each count of a third-degree felony is punishable by up to five years in prison, up to five years' probation and a fine of up to $5,000. Investigators said their actions demonstrated a "committed, willful failure or omission to provide a child with the care, supervision, and services necessary to maintain the child's physical and mental health, including but not limited to, food, nutrition, clothing, shelter, supervision, medicine and medical services that a prudent person would consider essential to the wellbeing of the child."

According to court documents, "capital sexual battery charges" against Stewart will be filed in the "9th Judicial District by the Statewide Prosecutor," a report shows. Under Florida law, anyone convicted of sexual battery of a child younger than 12 years old can face the death penalty or life in prison without parole.

All information about the children was redacted from reports, including their sexes, ages and relationships to each other and to Epps and Stewart. Epps and Stewart are being held in the Duval County Jail awaiting trial. Bond was set at $400,012 for Epps. Stewart was being held without bond.

title: Opinion - Tuesday’s election results could spell real trouble for Florida Republicans
description: Did Angie victory "hand Republicans a November Gift”? Quite the opposite.
fullText:
There was a political earthquake in Florida on Tuesday evening that could create prediction-shifting tremors — not only up until the midterm elections, but right through the 2028 presidential election. That earthquake was personified by far-left Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), who absolutely crushed Alex Vindman, the Democratic Party's sanctioned and favored candidate.

The morning after, while I was still trying to wrap my mind around the shocking upset, I came across a piece from RealClearPolitics titled: "Florida Democrats Hand Republicans a November Gift." I believe the message of the headline is way off the mark. For me — and for several Republican operatives I spoke with this week — Nixon's decisive victory represents a neon red warning sign for Florida Republicans.

In recent years, many pundits have claimed Florida to be "deep red" politically. I don't believe that to be the case. I do believe Gov. Ron DeSantis has proven himself to be an exceptional governor, saving the state from the draconian dictates rolled out during the COVID-19 pandemic. But unfortunately for the Republican Party, DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Neither is his highly capable wife, Casey DeSantis — a woman who, at one point, was considered a lock to succeed her husband, had she chosen to run.

It was not to be, and Tuesday just made it official. The Republican nominee for governor is Rep. Byron Donalds (R), the handpicked candidate of President Trump. And handpicked or not, Donalds may be sailing into some turbulent water.

The first sign is that although Donalds won the primary, a majority of Republicans voted for other candidates. One reason was the devastating ads challenger Jay Collins ran against him — ads that Democrats will ensure have a second life from now until November.

I have spoken with numerous Republicans in Florida, and none wanted Donalds as the nominee. Not one. Is that indicative of how the election will go in November? Maybe not, but these are Republicans who desperately want to keep Florida red.

Next is the victory by state Rep. Angie Nixon (D). Give her some props — Vindman and the entrenched Democratic Party outspent her about 16 to one, and she still humiliated him. But is her victory more about her strengths and connection with voters, or is it part of the growing voter dissatisfaction — and outright anger with incumbents — that we see sprouting up across the country? If it is the latter, which I believe it is, then that also spells trouble for Donalds and the Republican Party of Florida.

Not only is Nixon the new, new thing but Donalds is part of the old, old thing — most especially for young voters, the working class, and non-white voters. Rising star or not, Nixon is going to bring out a bunch of new voters. And even if they may not be able to put her over the top against Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), they will likely vote against Donalds while checking the box for Nixon.

It has been reported that there are 1.5 million more registered Republicans in Florida than Democrats. On paper, that seems to signal a slam-dunk for Donalds. But not so fast. A certain percentage of that 1.5 million identified as Republicans only because of support for DeSantis. Some share will stay home since DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Some of them are angry with Trump for endorsing Donalds and not giving Casey DeSantis the proper time or respect to evaluate a potential run. Some share aren't very impressed with Donalds, as the primary results demonstrate.

Nixon got more than 700,000 votes during the Democratic primary in deep red Florida.  Only a fool would underestimate her potential in the general. The promise of free stuff has worked since the invention of politics. Pardon the pun, but that promise will partially trump Trump and his various endorsements.

While not running against him, Nixon will still be an X factor in the eventual Donalds vote total — one that doesn't even take into account Democratic primary winner for governor David Jolly, nor how much money the national party will pour into Florida.

So did the Nixon victory "hand Republicans a November Gift"? Quite the opposite. I believe it has energized the Democratic base in the state while opening more eyes to the possibility that Florida is not as nearly as red as some have come to believe.

Donalds was mostly off the voter radar screen as a congressman. But now that he is the Republican nominee for governor, he is going to come under increased scrutiny. The betting odds may still list him as the favorite come November, but no one I know will be shocked if he goes down to defeat.

If I were the Republican leadership, I would cut out the personal attack nonsense and start addressing the issues that most matter to the working class.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

title: 8 South Florida cities among 'worst' real estate markets in state, says new report
description: South Florida cities are among the worst real estate markets in the state, according to a new study by WalletHub.
fullText:
Miami Beach is among the worst real estate markets in the U.S., according to a new study by WalletHub — within the state itself, markets in South Florida populate the lower ranks.

In the Aug. 19 report, the personal finance company evaluated 300 cities of "varying sizes" across "two key dimensions" — real estate market, along with affordability and economic environment. WalletHub "evaluated those dimensions using 17 relevant metrics" in order to "determine the best local real estate markets."

The full list of metrics, which were assigned various weights, can be found at the bottom of the report. They include characteristics such as home value forecast, median days on the market, share of seriously underwater mortgages and ratio of rent price to sale price. Each metric was "graded on a 100-point scale, with a score of 100 representing the healthiest housing market."

Among the 300 cities surveyed, Miami Beach ranked as number 294, with a total score of 39.33. The city had a real-estate market rank of 293 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 228.

In Florida alone, Miami Beach ranks at the bottom, followed by Hollywood, which ranked 285th overall. The latter city received a total score of 43.13, with a real-estate market rank of 283 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 170.

Other South Florida cities among the bottom two hundred included West Palm Beach, which ranked at 241 with a total score of 48.75, Sunrise, which ranked at 244 with a total score of 48.41 and Pompano Beach, which ranked at 271 with a total score of 45.74.

The Miami market itself, however, ranked among the top 40 nationally. At number 38, the city had a total score of 60.28, a real-estate market rank of 30 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 167. It was also the most highly ranked Florida market.

"Current home prices are extremely important, but there's much more that you need to look at when determining the health of a city's real estate market," said Chip Lupo, an analyst for WalletHub. "Factors like the cost of living, the potential for the value of homes to increase, the availability of recently-built homes and the quality of the city's job market are all important to consider in conjunction with asking prices and interest rates."

title: Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon defends drag shows as 'wholesome' for children, brought her kids to one
description: Democratic socialist Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon defended drag shows as "wholesome entertainment," saying she has taken her own children to them.
fullText:
Democratic socialist Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, who recently won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, blasted the idea of restricting children's access to drag shows, and called such entertainment "wholesome" during an interview in August.

During a sit-down with Nixon on the "Legal AF" podcast, Melba Pearson, a criminal law expert and civil rights advocate, appeared to conflate Florida's Parental Rights in Education law, which concerns children's education, with the Protection of Children Act that restricts minors' access to drag shows.

"I believe it was today or yesterday, the appeals court upheld that, the law that basically we call 'Don't Say Gay,' that the biggest provision that everybody's most familiar with is that it makes it illegal for anyone under 18 to be at a drag show," Melba said. "So basically it's criminalizing drag in a lot of ways, right? And so, you know, in seeing that, what does that tell you and how can you translate that into policy, you know, when you get to D.C.?"

"Yeah, for sure. What that is telling me is that there's an attack on an 'othering' of people who don't look like Donald Trump. Like, right?" Nixon said. "Like, it is just an attack on marginalized communities. They want to create this country that looks a certain way, that acts a certain way, that believes a certain way. And it's frustrating."

Federal Appeals Court Clears Way For Desantis-backed Law Restricting Children At Some Drag Shows

She went on to defend drag shows as "wholesome entertainment," saying she has taken her own children to shows.

"I don't understand, like, there's no sexualization at a drag show! It's just people dressing up and singing and performing! I've taken my children to drag shows, and it's fun! It's entertainment," she said. "It's wholesome entertainment and it's nothing wrong. It's just like, I don't get it."

Theo Wold, former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under President Donald Trump, told Fox News Digital that Nixon's statement was inaccurate.

"Drag has always been sexualized entertainment — that's why it originated in bars and nightclubs in front of adult audiences. On one hand, DSA candidates like Rashida Tlaib endorsed Angie Nixon, want to Islamify America by opening our borders, and electing radical Muslim clerics to high office, especially our courts; on the other hand, they want to bring drag performers to kids," he said.

"It doesn't make sense until you understand their larger project, which is to destabilize Western civilization — whether by undermining our legal regime or by destabilizing the nuclear family," he said.

Senate Hopeful Says Texas Home To The 'Best Drag Queens In The Nation' In Resurfaced Comments

Curtis Houck, the managing editor of the NewsBusters division of the Media Research Center, suggested that certain news networks will desperately try to avoid covering Nixon's comments.

"Needless to say, it's doubtful this will be a comment that's played on the regular across the liberal, elitist networks like ABC or CNN in the months to come as proof she's outside the mainstream," Houck said.

"It's a completely cockamamie claim that, if the so-called fact-checkers like Politifact were honest brokers, they would have already penned an item with a pants-on-fire rating. The only thing that's 'wholesome' about drag shows is how wholly sexual they are. Even those who support that kind of thing should be able to acknowledge that. What a grotesque commentary on the left that someone like her would want young children to attend drag shows," Houck added.

Founder of Gays Against Groomers, Jaimee Michell, condemned Nixon's statements of drag shows being wholesome family events as "dangerous" lies.

"Angie Nixon's comments are a lie, and a dangerous one," Michell told Fox News Digital.

"There is no shortage of video of drag performers in pasties, thongs, or barely-there costumes grinding, twerking, and simulating sex in front of children — including babies and toddlers — while those kids are encouraged to stuff dollar bills into their outfits. That is not 'people dressing up and singing.' That is adult sexual performance. Calling it 'wholesome entertainment' is gaslighting," she said.

Michell also said that the practice of drag was inherently sexual and built on "exaggerated, hyper-sexualized parody of women."

"Nixon taking her own children to these shows does not make it wholesome. It makes her judgment a warning," she added. "Florida passed a law to keep minors out of lewd live performances for a reason. This is not about banning adults from performing. It is about whether we are going to keep pretending that exposing kids to nearly nude adults collecting tips is just 'fun.' It isn't.

"Nixon is wrong, the footage proves it, and Florida voters already know it," Michell said.

Nixon, a progressive activist and DSA member, defeated establishment-backed candidate and retired Air Force officer Alexander Vindman by more than 10 percentage points despite Vindman's $16.3 million campaign war chest, compared with Nixon's roughly $1 million.

Nixon will now face Trump-backed Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., in November for the right to serve the remaining two years of Rubio's Senate term.

title: Surprise election upset shows hating Trump is no longer enough as Democratic voters turn to new playbook
description: Alexander Vindman, a key witness in Trump's first impeachment, lost Florida's Democratic Senate primary to a socialist by double digits.
fullText:
A growing number of Democrats who grabbed national attention as they led the resistance to President Donald Trump during his first term in the White House are the latest casualties in this year's primary battle between the party's left-wing and the establishment.

The latest victim: Alexander Vindman, who gained national prominence nearly a decade ago as the then-Army lieutenant colonel and National Security Council official who served as a key witness against Trump during the president's first impeachment trial.

Vindman, who made resisting Trump a key part of his Senate bid, was upset Tuesday in Florida's Democratic Senate primary by state Rep. Angie Nixon. A Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member, Nixon landed a double-digit victory over Vindman despite being outspent by a roughly 10-to-1 margin.

His defeat, as well as losses to challengers from the far-left by other one-time resistance stars such as Reps. Diana DeGette of Colorado and Dan Goldman of New York, appear to point to shifting priorities for a Democratic base moving left, starving for change and eager to use midterm election victories to escape the political wilderness.

Also falling short so far this primary season are Reps. Shri Thanedar of Michigan and Al Green of Texas, who led the Trump impeachment pushes. They both went down to younger challengers. Meanwhile, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, who was a member of key committees handling Trump's second impeachment in 2021, fell short as he bid for the Senate.

A congressional run by longtime Trump critic George Conway, a co-founder of the anti-Trump Republican group the Lincoln Project, failed to ignite. And former U.S. Capitol Police Officer Harry Dunn, who was honored for his efforts during the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, lost for a second straight cycle as he campaigned for a congressional seat in Maryland.

Veteran Democratic political commentator Ben Rhodes, who served as a leading official in former President Barack Obama's administration, has repeatedly argued that opposition to Trump is insufficient to build a lasting political movement. He has emphasized that to win at the ballot box, Democrats must articulate how they'll help address voters' economic concerns and day-to-day frustrations.

Shannon Jackson, a longtime progressive political strategist and grassroots organizer best known for his leadership roles in Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, told Fox News Digital that "it's not enough anymore just to oppose Trump."

Referring to the onetime resistance leaders who lost their primaries this year, Jackson said, "They've stood up to Trump, but the fact is it's not enough anymore. We need to recognize why Trump won, we need to recognize the failings of the Democratic Party and the Democratic leaders who have gotten us to this point, and we need to improve upon it."

Jackson, a top consultant for progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, said, "what really happened is that we've seen the progressive movement succeed… it's an entire wave that's coming across the country."

Longtime strategist and political commentator Maria Cardona, a DNC committee member, told Fox News Digital she doesn't buy the narrative that "huge heroes of Trump resistance one are just not cutting it anymore."

"Voters want someone who is going to fight for them. Whether or not you call yourself establishment, a moderate, a progressive, or DSA, voters don't care. Voters want to see you fighting for them," Cardona emphasized.

Cardona said "whether you are a Abdul El-Sayed, who is new on the scene, or a Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who has been there for decades but who has delivered for her community and is still seen as a fighter, you're going to win. You have to deliver. That's the secret."

title: Florida high school QB returns to football after leukemia battle, 20 months after last game
description: A leukemia diagnosis sidelined Carter Quinn for his senior season. After an appeal, he's been granted a fifth year of high school football, which starts Friday night.
fullText:
NAPLES, FL — By the time Friday, Aug. 21, rolls around, Carter Quinn will have spent nearly two years waiting to do something that used to be so ordinary he never thought twice about it.

He'll put on a football uniform. He'll walk onto a field. He'll take the first snap of the game at quarterback for St. John Neumann (FL).

And then he'll wait for the whistle.

Quinn knows what happens after that. The other team won't care that he spent months in a hospital. It won't care that chemotherapy took more than 50 pounds from his body or that there was a time when he wasn't sure he'd ever play football again. It won't care about the fifth-year waiver that had to be approved for him to get here.

"I mean, I think I'll definitely take it in for a second, but once the ref blows the whistle, you've got to lock in," Carter said. "No one's thinking about what you've been through or what's going on. Everybody on the other team is just trying to do what they can to win, so no one's thinking about how you feel or what you went through."

For Quinn, that whistle has been a long time coming.

The last time he heard it in a meaningful game, he was still a junior at Lely and a quarterback whose biggest concern was what might come next. He had just thrown for 304 yards and four touchdowns and run for another 71 yards and a score in a 90-56 win over Barron Collier. College football was beginning to enter the conversation. His future, at least as he understood it then, seemed to be opening up in front of him.

Quinn played through it. He finished Lely's season, even though his father, Steve Quinn, knew something wasn't right. After the Trojans lost to Miami Northwestern in the playoffs on Nov. 22, Carter went to have the knee examined.

The ACL tear they found wasn't the biggest problem. The bloodwork was.

His blood-cell count was high. The doctor told the family there were several possibilities, one of which was leukemia. The doctor estimated the odds at 1-to-2%. The family didn't think much of it. There was no history of leukemia in the family, and the possibility seemed remote enough that they went about their lives.

Three weeks later, on Dec. 17, Steve and Carter's mother Lori Quinn were at the Paradise Coast Sports Complex when the doctor called. They were in a staff meeting, and Lori stepped outside to take the call. Steve didn't know what she had heard yet, but he knew something was wrong when he watched his wife fall to the ground.

"I just remember her falling to the ground, and I knew something was wrong," Steve said.

The 1-to-2% possibility they had tried not to think about was no longer a possibility. Carter had leukemia.

That night, Steve and Lori had to tell their son. The next morning, he would begin chemotherapy.

Carter didn't really understand what leukemia meant. His experience with cancer was mostly what he had seen in movies, so the diagnosis hadn't yet taken on the meaning it would later carry. His mind went instead to the thing that had occupied so much of his life.

"'Can I play spring football?' That's the first thing I asked (the doctor)," Carter recalls. "He just kind of looked at me funny. I didn't really know what it was."

He would learn quickly enough. The next 18 months brought spinal taps, lumbar punctures, intravenous chemotherapy and medications designed to fight the abnormal blood cells. Hospital stays became part of the routine, with one standing rule: If Carter's temperature reached 101 degrees, he had to go back.

Steve remembers one such night particularly well. Carter had been home for only two hours after spending four or five days in the hospital when his temperature reached 101. They had to take him back. Remarkably, Steve said, that was the only time during the entire process he remembers his son complaining.

"He just did the deal," Steve said. "He never, ever complained. The only time — one time — he complained was when he just got home from the hospital. He was there for four or five days, and anytime he got to a 101-degree temperature, he had to go to the hospital. He literally got home, and within two hours he got a 101-degree temperature, and we had to take him back.

"That's the only time I ever heard him complain during these 18 months. He was just a trooper."

The physical changes were harder for Carter to ignore. He had been playing at roughly 190 pounds at Lely. During treatment, he eventually fell to about 138. A few months into it, he began to realize just how much his body had changed.

"A little bit later, a couple months into treatment, I kind of realized, 'Dang, my body's changing,'" Carter said. "There were definitely thoughts of, 'I don't think I'll ever play the game again.' Once the idea of the extra year came, it kind of was there, but there was definitely a big period where I didn't think I'd ever play football again."

For a while, there wasn't much Carter could do about those thoughts. His body needed to recover, and football had to wait. But stepping away from the game entirely was never really an option for him.

When Lely's 2025 season arrived, Carter couldn't play. His younger brother Brady, who transferred from First Baptist, could, and Carter wanted to be around him and the program. So he kept showing up at practices, usually in a Lely jacket and sweats, and looked for ways to contribute. Former Lely coach Ben Hammer gave him a headset, and Carter began helping where he could — offering encouragement, pointing out small things and occasionally coaching Brady, who was two years younger.

It wasn't a formal coaching assignment. Carter wanted to help, Hammer said, and the headset gave him a way to remain involved with the team he had spent the previous season leading on the field.

There were days when even that was difficult. The effects of chemotherapy sometimes made it hard for Carter to put on tennis shoes, so Hammer made an exception to one of his standing practice rules. Nobody was supposed to show up in slides or flip-flops. Carter still wanted to be at practice, though, and Hammer wasn't going to let a rule keep him away.

"He still wanted to be at practice, to be around his brothers," Hammer said. "And when I say his brother, not just his actual brother, but mentor Luke Trebilcock, our JV quarterback, and help with that young but talented wide receiver crew we had."

For Carter, being around the team offered something that treatment couldn't. He couldn't take a snap, but he could still talk football. He could watch Brady. He could help younger players. He could remain connected to the routine and the people that had been such a large part of his life before his diagnosis.

Hammer came to see that as part of Carter's recovery, too.

"And I think that he would tell you that that was part of his healing process," Hammer said. "And, for lack of a better term, like, the winning process against leukemia was being at Lely football every day and how much his friends and buddies did to kind of encourage him and keep him going in the right direction."

Carter's presence also became a reminder of what the Lely program had been missing. He was still the quarterback everyone knew, only now he was watching from the sideline instead of taking the snaps. His friends didn't let him disappear completely. Lely began putting orange, football-shaped stickers on their helmets with CQ8 printed in black — a small tribute to Carter's initials and the No. 8 he had always worn. That ultimately spread to neighboring high schools.

Brady wore the number himself during the 2025 season for his brother.

His decision to remain at Lely carried its own significance. Brady had opportunities to attend a national-level football program, Hammer said, but chose to stay with his brother and family during a difficult period. Carter couldn't play, but his brother was still wearing his number and playing the game they had grown up around together.

For Carter, that season offered an unusual version of football. He wasn't competing. He wasn't preparing for college recruiting. He was simply trying to get healthy enough to have another chance.

For much of that winter, there was no clear indication of when — or whether — Carter would look like that player again. His focus was on getting through treatment. Football remained important, but for the first time in his life, it was something he could only watch from the outside.

For a long time, getting back to football was something Carter could only imagine. Then, in the spring, the possibility began to feel more tangible.

On March 2, 2026 Carter had his port removed. He was still undergoing treatment, but doctors told him that if his platelets and hemoglobin were where they needed to be, he could begin working out and lifting again, eventually progressing to contact football. After spending so long watching his body become weaker, Carter finally had something concrete to work toward.

"As soon as they told him that he was free and cleared to play, you just could tell the look in his eye was all different," Steve Quinn said. "He just was motivated."

Football wasn't the only thing that helped him get through the months when he couldn't play. Through Make-A-Wish, Carter received a boat, giving him a way to spend time on the water with his family and another activity that didn't require him to push his recovering body the way football would. Fishing became something he could look forward to, while the possibility of returning to the field remained somewhere in the distance.

"I would say just being on the water is really peaceful," Carter said. "It's kind of something you can do when it's not getting tackled by the linemen and stuff. Something that also kept my mind off of it was the fact that I would have the chance to play football again if it did come through, and just to keep pushing through because the end goal was to play football again and keep going after all my dreams. It was the fact that I had that in the back of my mind, that I could do it again."

"The first couple months, we really had to take it slow and just get my body back," Carter said. "But once it started kicking, we were just full go. He's been with me for the nutrition part, just spiritually, mentally, and he's just been there step by step. He puts his focus on me and just walks me through it. He's the person who really got my body back to what it was."

The progress became measurable. Carter began eating three meals a day, something that hadn't always been possible during treatment, and started putting weight back on. He threw regularly with Ken Mastrole, a quarterbacks coach in Southwest Florida, and continued lifting as his body allowed. By August, he was up to 179 pounds, just 11 pounds shy of where he had been when he was playing for Lely.

"When I started working out again, I started at like 145 pounds, I think, and now I'm up to 179 as of yesterday," Carter said. "Just putting muscle on, putting weight on and eating healthy, treating my body like a temple and all that. Like I said, not taking nothing for granted."

Carter still wants to get back to 190. But he's not necessarily chasing the exact version of himself who played at Lely. He believes the body he's rebuilding may ultimately be different from the one he had before leukemia.

"I think I was a lot thicker playing at Lely, but I think I have a lot more cut muscle," Carter said. "If I'm at 185 to 187, I'll be okay with that."

That process became another part of the comeback. Lely principal Jennifer Bledsoe and Hammer worked with legendary Naples head coach Bill Kramer, who went up to Gainesville in person to lobby on Quinn's behalf, while Carter's family gathered what was needed to make its case. After spending so much of the previous year having little control over what his body could do, Carter was now waiting on a group of people he'd never met to decide whether he could play the game he had spent his life preparing for.

The hearing was held April 8. Carter, Steve, Lori and Sean Phillips, a close friend who had a hand in getting him the boat, gathered for a Zoom meeting with a sectional committee within the FHSAA. They answered questions and explained Carter's circumstances, then waited while the committee considered the request.

The meeting lasted about 15 minutes.

Then a motion was made to approve Carter's fifth year. There was a very quick second.

After 18 months of wondering whether football was gone from his life for good, Carter had his answer.

"I was really happy," Carter said. "I kind of had the feeling I knew I was going to get it because Miss Bledsoe and Coach Hammer worked really hard and worked with Coach Kramer, who used to be on that board. They worked really hard to help me get it, but it was just a relief because I knew I would get my life back on track."

That last part is what mattered most to Carter. The fifth year wasn't simply another season on a football schedule. It gave him back a routine he had lost when leukemia took him away from the field. Shortly after the ruling was made, he made an announcement that he'd be transferring to St. John Neumann.

"Football, it's always been football, so that's all I know," Carter said. "It was kind of getting back into that routine of working out and then playing, so I was just really happy."

Steve had watched the entire process from a different perspective. He had watched people rally around his son when Carter couldn't play, then watched Carter rebuild his body when doctors finally allowed him to return to physical activity. Now, after all the uncertainty, the answer was no longer dependent on what might happen. Carter had been given another season.

Steve remembers his son's reaction being much simpler than the months of work that had gone into getting there.

For Carter, the approval didn't erase what had happened. He was still undergoing treatment, and his doctors would not consider him officially in remission until a later point in the process. It didn't put the weight back on his frame overnight or turn him immediately into the quarterback he'd been at Lely.

What it did was give him something he had spent months without: a date to work toward.

And this time, there was a football field at the end of it.

In July, Carter finally got to do something he had spent more than a year imagining: He walked onto a football practice field wearing a helmet again.

Not a headset. Not a Lely jacket and sweats. A helmet.

And at St. John Neumann, there was no competition for the quarterback job. It was Carter's.

The routine he had once taken for granted had become the thing he had worked toward for months. Conditioning. Lifting. Throwing. Walking into a locker room with teammates. Getting pushed hard by a coach. All of it had taken on a different meaning after spending so much time away from it.

"You're not taking anything for granted," Carter said. "You used to be like, 'Oh, we're conditioning,' and now you're like, 'Damn, it is awesome that you get to be out here.' You never think about how much you would just like being around the guys in the locker room when you're not. You don't think about the little things, and now you just appreciate everything. When something's taken away from you, it just makes you realize so much."

The quarterback wearing No. 8 is also different from the one who wore it at Lely. After the tributes with helmet stickers and his brother wearing the number, it's now back on Carter, who has spent the entire summer preparing to start again.

The football return, however, has come before the medical journey is officially finished. Carter said he currently has no cancer cells in his body, but his doctors won't technically consider him in remission until he reaches the required point in his treatment. For now, he is taking pills and continuing to follow the treatment plan that began after his diagnosis in December 2024.

That reality has changed Carter's perspective on what it means to return. Before leukemia, football was simply what he did. Now, after having it taken away, he understands how much of his life was wrapped up in things he barely noticed.

Steve has noticed the change, too. The son who went through treatment is not the same teenager who entered his junior season at Lely, and the difference has little to do with how much weight Carter has regained or how well he throws a football.

"He has become a different kid," Steve said. "I can't imagine what has gone through his head over the last 18 months, but his maturity level and his awareness and just who he is as a person has totally changed."

That may be the biggest difference between the quarterback who left the field against Barron Collier and the one who will return Friday night.

The first time Carter played after his diagnosis won't be about proving that he beat leukemia. He hasn't reached that point yet. It won't be about proving that he can be the same quarterback he was before, either. His body is different, his perspective is different and his life has changed in ways that can't be measured by passing yards or touchdowns.

It will simply be another football game.

St. John Neumann will host Monsignor Pace of Miami at 7:30 p.m. Friday. Carter will take the first snap at quarterback, something that once would have been so routine that he never would have thought twice about it.

He knows what it is like to stand on the outside and watch somebody else play. He knows what it is like to wonder if he'll ever get the chance again.

And he knows that once the whistle blows, none of that matters to the other team.

"It's like everybody's playing for themselves, really," Carter Quinn said. "There's no sympathy for me on the field, so that's why I've got to get back to that point where I can be that guy that I was and go just tear it up."

For nearly two years, Carter has been waiting for that whistle.

Friday night, he'll finally hear it again.

title: Where Florida football lands in preseason bowl projections
description: Florida football is projected to face off against an in-state rival in CBS Sports' preseason bowl projections.
fullText:
The Florida Gators look to return to the postseason after missing a bowl game for the fourth time since 2013 last season.

Florida has controlled most of their matchups in the past, but a potential bowl matchup would also mark the first meeting between Florida and South Florida in the Sumrall era and would give the Gators a chance to get back on track against the in-state opponent.

title: Trump celebrates Florida loss of ‘treasonous creep’
description: President Trump on Wednesday celebrated the loss of Alex Vindman in the Senate Democratic primary in Florida. “The most gratifying loss last night was that of a real treasonous creep, Alexander Vindma...
fullText:
President Trump on Wednesday celebrated the loss of Alex Vindman in the Senate Democratic primary in Florida.

"The most gratifying loss last night was that of a real treasonous creep, Alexander Vindman, to a Radical Left Lunatic, who can't speak or think properly," Trump wrote on Truth Social, referring to Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), who defeated Vindman by more than 12 points on Tuesday.

Vindman, a retired Army lieutenant colonel and former director of European affairs for the National Security Council, rose to national prominence as a witness during Trump's first impeachment trial.

Vindman testified to Congress about his concerns regarding Trump pressing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to investigate former President Biden. Trump claimed his request to Zelensky was part of a "perfect" call, a defense he again brought up on Wednesday.

"Vindman, if you remember, was the one who lied about my 'Perfect Call' with President Zelenskyy of Ukraine, only to find out that the conversation was routinely recorded and proved that I was 100% in the right (Completely Innocent!)," the president added.

Trump also wrote Vindman, the twin brother of Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Va.), "should be prosecuted" for his testimony. The Senate acquitted the president on both articles of impeachment, the first of Trump's two impeachment trials overseen by the upper chamber.

As for Nixon, the president wrote she will "go down to certain defeat" to GOP Sen. Ashley Moody (Fla.), whom Trump called "truly Fantastic."

Moody, whom Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) appointed to succeed Secretary of State Marco Rubio, will face Nixon in a special election to determine who will serve the remaining two years of Rubio's term.

Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, defeated Vindman despite a significant fundraising disadvantage. As of July 29, Nixon's campaign had less than $265,000 on hand, while Vindman's had more than $7.2 million, according to the Federal Election Commission.

With the Moody-Nixon match-up set, election handicapper Sabato's Crystal Ball shifted the race to the right on Wednesday — from "likely Republican" to "safely Republican."

title: Florida Democrat sends 'condolences' to Hasan Piker after defeating DSA challenger in Florida primary
description: Rep. Jared Moskowitz sent "condolences" to Hasan Piker on X after defeating DSA-backed Oliver Larkin in Florida's 25th District Democratic primary.
fullText:
Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz took a victory lap on X Tuesday after he was declared the winner over a democratic socialist challenger in Florida's congressional primary, sending mocking "condolences" to Hasan Piker, a far-left streamer who backed Moskowitz's opponent.

Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-backed Oliver Larkin lost to the more moderate Moskowitz in the Democratic primary in Florida's 25th District, The Associated Press reported.

The heavily redrawn congressional swing district is among roughly two dozen House seats that will likely determine whether Republicans hold on to their razor-thin majority in the midterm elections.

"My condolences to @hasanthehun," Moskowitz wrote on X.

Pro-israel Moderate Survives Primary Challenge By Socialist Insurgent

Piker responded to Moskowitz's callout on X and wrote, "its pretty wild that his first thought was a prominent critic of israel, before even thanking his constituents lmao. really worried about his genocidal emotional support apartheid state."

Moskowitz thanked his constituents on Wednesday in another post to X.

"I want to thank the voters of District 25 for continuing to have the faith in me to deliver results for Florida," he wrote. "I want to thank my wife and kids who I have spent a lot of time away from. My dad died of cancer 4 years ago. He would have enjoyed all of this. I miss him. Onward!"

Moskowitz's campaign did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"Democrats shouldn't play hide the Piker now," Moskowitz said after his victory, according to Politico Playbook. "For all those people who thought it was a great idea to campaign with him, as Jay-Z once said, 'Bring 'em out, bring 'em out.' They shouldn't be hiding him now."

Piker hit back in a comment to Playbook and said, "I'm genuinely concerned for his mental well-being."

"I think he should stop posting on the internet and focus on defeating the Republican in his newly redistricted congressional seat," Piker added, according to the outlet. Moskowitz then called DSA members "anti-American at their core."

Who Is Hasan Piker? Meet The Far-left Streamer Who Is Stirring Up Controversy And Dividing Democrats

Piker has been a political flashpoint within the Democratic Party, as a debate over whether the party should embrace or distance itself from the streamer has taken shape.

The streamer has campaigned with far-left candidates, including Francesca Hong, who lost her gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, among others.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said during an interview in early August that the party should include people like Piker, and said that the streamer reaches a lot of voters. Others, like Democratic strategist James Carville, have said they don't want to belong to the same political party as Piker.

Commentator Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that Piker would likely be taking a similar victory lap had Larkin won the race.

"One of the asymmetries in Democratic politics right now is that when a DSA candidate wins, it is immediately treated as evidence of some enormous ideological realignment in the party," Shroff said. "When a more moderate Democrat wins, there is usually much less hype and almost no corresponding narrative.

"We saw that with David Crowley beating Francesca Hong in Wisconsin, and now Moskowitz has beaten a DSA-backed challenger in Florida," Shroff continued. "Imagine the coverage if the result had gone the other way, and imagine the victory lap Hasan Piker and the online left would be taking right now.

"I actually think there is value in Moskowitz picking this fight," he added. "Piker backed his opponent and made himself part of the race. By going after him publicly, Moskowitz is forcing people to tell the other side of this story, and, frankly, here we are talking about it because he did."

title: After Trump-endorsed Cory Mills loses primary, Trump says he told him to drop out
description: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he had urged GOP Rep. Cory Mills to drop out of his Florida primary race before the embattled Republican lost Tuesday to former news anchor Ryan Elijah.
fullText:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he had urged GOP Rep. Cory Mills to drop out of his Florida primary race before the embattled Republican lost Tuesday to former news anchor Ryan Elijah.

"I told Congressman Cory Mills of Florida, a friend of mine, to get out of the Race, but he wouldn't listen. He thought he could win, so who can blame him?" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Trump endorsed Mills in February and never publicly rescinded his support, despite the Florida congressman facing significant scrutiny over accusations of assault, potential campaign finance violations and an ex-girlfriend alleging that he threatened to release sexually explicit images and videos of her. Mills has denied any wrongdoing.

However, the congressman was conspicuously absent from a list Trump posted earlier this month of Florida Republicans he endorsed. The president also did not participate in tele-rallies on his behalf, which he's done for several lawmakers he supports.

Mills wouldn't be the first embattled GOP congressman who Trump leaned on to quit. The president told Ohio Rep. Max Miller — whose ex-wife has accused him of abuse — in a previously reported call that he was going to lose his election and lose for the Republican Party if he kept up his reelection bid, according to two sources briefed on the call. CNN previously reported that Trump had expressed that sentiment to some allies, but not that the president said as much to Miller directly.

The Ohio Republican has denied wrongdoing and downplayed the call with Trump in public comments. He told CNN's Jake Tapper that the president told him it would be a "tough race," and that he didn't know "that you're going to be able to pull this one out."

In the social media post distancing himself from Mills, Trump also endorsed Ryan Elijah, who will now advance as the Republican candidate following his primary victory on Tuesday night.

"We now have a great candidate, Ryan Elijah, running in his place! Ryan stands for EVERYTHING MAGA, and is respected by ALL. He has my Complete and Total Endorsement!" Trump wrote.

A defiant Mills not only refused to drop out of the race, but told CNN in April that he would not resign from Congress despite calls from some Republicans to step down amid the allegations of sexual misconduct.

"There's absolutely no reason to resign," Mills told CNN at the time, adding that House Speaker Mike Johnson had told him in conversations not to give up his seat. "He told me not to resign, and he told me that this is why we have this process."

Johnson did not directly confirm the exchange to CNN but said Mills should be afforded due process. Johnson also declined to say whether he would support Mills' reelection bid.

The Ethics Committee is currently looking into multiple allegations made against Mills, including campaign finance violations and sexual misconduct. The Florida congressman has also been under investigation by DC police for allegedly assaulting an individual.

He was also previously ordered by a judge not to have any contact with the ex-girlfriend who accused the congressman of having threatened to release sexually explicit images and videos of her after their relationship ended.

Mills was not the only Trump-endorsed candidate to suffer a primary defeat Tuesday night. Catalina Lauf in Florida and Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming also lost their respective races, underscoring that Trump's endorsement does not necessarily guarantee that voters will back his preferred candidates.

In Florida, Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos had already broken with Mills, endorsing Elijah earlier this month.

Now, after decisively defeating Mills and with the backing of the president, Elijah will advance as the Republican nominee.

title: Veteran Dem defeats scandal-plagued former lawmaker, progressive challenger in Trump's backyard
description: Debbie Wasserman Schultz faced a progressive challenger and fraud-accused ex-lawmaker in Florida's 20th Congressional District Democratic primary.
fullText:
Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz has bested a young progressive challenger and an embattled former lawmaker after a hard-fought primary characterized by its racial overtones.

Schultz, a 21-year veteran of the House, stressed her seniority on the campaign trail and her ability to deliver services to constituents and secure federal funding for her district.

To secure her primary victory, Schultz defeated former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who resigned in April following fraud allegations, and 27-year-old activist and teacher Elijah Manley, who is aligned with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party.

Jeffries Declines To Back Wasserman Schultz As Black Leaders Revolt Over District Switch

Mid-decade redistricting in Florida prompted Schultz to choose to run in Florida's 20th Congressional District, which has a stronger Democratic lean than her home constituency.

Schultz, a White woman, drew considerable backlash for deciding to run in the district in May. Criticism centered around the district being majority Black and having long been represented by a Black member of Congress.

Both Cherfilus-McCormick and Manley argued that Schultz representing Florida's 20th Congressional District would be an affront to the African American community. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries declined to back Schultz during the dispute.

"While the Republicans are trying their hardest to silence Black voices, I don't expect somebody in our own party, a White Democrat, to do the same," Manley said of Schultz at a candidate debate. "We are not going back to a time where there were no Black people in Congress."

Tlaib Under Fire For Working To Unseat Two Jewish House Democrats In Florida: 'No Coincidence'

Cherfilus-McCormick accused Schultz of "district forum shopping" and said electing her would amount to the erasure of Black history and power.

During a debate, Schultz defended her candidacy by emphasizing her extensive tenure in Congress and her experience representing Black and Caribbean communities in her former district.

Cherfilus-McCormick's candidacy was itself mired in controversy.

Federal prosecutors say Cherfilus-McCormick and her co-defendants stole a $5 million overpayment from a FEMA-funded COVID-19 vaccination contract, laundered the money through multiple accounts and used part of it to finance her 2021 congressional campaign through illegal contributions. She resigned from Congress in April before an expulsion vote could be scheduled and has pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.

Former Bernie Sanders Official Accuses Senator Of Pushing Most Antisemitic Candidates 'In A Generation'

Accusations that Schultz was carpetbagging and the federal fraud charges against Cherfilus-McCormick weren't the only controversies in the Democratic primary in Florida's 20th Congressional District.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib appeared at a Fort Lauderdale Chomp the Oligarchy rally Aug. 14 to support the effort to oust Schultz from Congress. Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., has claimed the effort to oust Schultz stems from the fact that she is Jewish.

Schultz has described herself as a "staunch supporter" of Israel and has voted against measures to cut off military aid. Her position has put her at odds with progressives seeking to reduce U.S. support for Israel.

Other candidates in the Democratic primary for Florida's 20th Congressional District included former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness and longtime community activist Luther "Uncle Luke" Campbell.

title: Renaming Florida's Palm Beach airport after Donald Trump cost an estimated $5.5 million. Take a look at the changes.
description: Florida's Palm Beach International Airport is now President Donald J. Trump International Airport, featuring new signage with the presidential seal.
fullText:
Florida's Palm Beach International Airport is now President Donald J. Trump International Airport.

The name changed on July 9, and its IATA code changed from "PBI" to "DJT" on August 18.

The change, including new signage with the presidential seal, will cost an estimated $5.5 million.

President Donald Trump has reportedly expressed interest in having an airport named after him since his first term in the White House.

During his second, non-consecutive term, he became the first sitting US president to see that happen: On July 9, Florida's Palm Beach International Airport officially became President Donald J. Trump International Airport.

While new signage has already gone up, the airport's International Air Transport Association, or IATA, code — used for ticketing, baggage, and flight information displays — remained "PBI" until it changed to "DJT" on Tuesday.

In a Truth Social post on July 9, Trump said it was a "Great Honor" to have the airport renamed after him, adding that it would "soon be one of the Greatest and Most Spectacular Airports anywhere in the World!"

The Palm Beach County Department of Airports estimated that the name change will cost around $5.5 million. State funding is financing $2.75 million of the project, and the Department of Airports "will continue to pursue all available funding sources" for the remaining cost, the airport said in a statement.

When asked how the name change has affected the airport's operations and passenger experience, a representative for President Donald J. Trump International Airport referred Business Insider to a statement on the airport's website.

"While we recognize that the required name change may be received in different ways by our passengers, we're grateful for your continued support through this transition period," the statement reads. "We remain committed to serving all passengers and ensuring a positive travel experience. While some things may evolve over time, our core focus remains the same: providing a safe, reliable, and welcoming airport experience."

Palm Beach's travel hub isn't the only airport undergoing changes during Trump's presidency.

On July 29, Trump unveiled his plan for a $22.5 billion renovation at Washington Dulles International Airport in Washington, DC, adding or renovating more than 5 million square feet and eliminating the airport's "people mover" shuttles, among other upgrades.

Take a look at the newly renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport.

On March 30, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a law renaming Palm Beach International Airport after President Donald Trump.

Workers began installing new signage in early July, ahead of the renaming.

On July 9, the airport officially debuted as President Donald J. Trump International Airport.

Highway signs on I-95 display the airport's new name.

Inside the airport, signage has also been updated to welcome passengers to President Donald J. Trump International Airport.

The airport's new logo resembles the presidential seal.

When printed in color, the new airport logo appears in gold — a color Trump is known to favor.

Notifications on screens displaying arrivals and departures also refer to the airport by its updated name.

On July 9, Trump's personal Boeing 757, known as "Trump Force One," became the first plane to land at the renamed airport at 5:01 a.m.

Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. flew in on Trump Force One to celebrate the change with Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter.

title: 'Hateful': Both parties slam House candidate Dan Bilzerian's antisemitic attacks
description: Dan Bilzerian is challenging Jewish Rep. Fine in Florida Republican primary.
fullText:
Politicians and elected officials from both parties are denouncing the onslaught of antisemitic postings, including posts directed at Jewish Republican Rep. Randy Fine by Dan Bilzerian, who is challenging Fine in Florida's 6th Congressional District.

While Bilzerian, an influencer, podcaster and businessman, has long spread provocative language and antisemitism, he has ramped up his rhetoric with a slew of antisemitic ads and verbal attacks targeting Fine. His content has also included references to Adolf Hitler and explicit antisemitic tropes.

Leaders from both parties in the House, Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, condemned Bilzerian's rhetoric and his candidacy Sunday evening.

"The vile attack ads against Congressman Randy Fine in Florida's 6th District are disgusting and should be condemned by all political leaders on the Right and Left. Antisemitism and outward hatred of Jewish communities have no place in our politics or in America, and we will continue to call them out wherever they arise," Johnson posted on X.

Jeffries similarly slammed the GOP candidate for his "hateful campaign," which he calls "blatantly antisemitic and shocks the conscience."

Republican Rep. Don Bacon and GOP Sen. Ted Cruz also expressed their revulsion, though Bilzerian remains undeterred and is using such criticism to further fuel his campaign.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also called Bilzerian's rhetoric "possibly the most disgusting political thread I've seen."

Fine, who won a special election last year to replace then-Rep. Mike Waltz when he resigned to become U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, has faced criticism over some of his remarks about Muslims and Palestinians.

In February Fine posted on X, "If they force us to choose, the choice between dogs and Muslims is not a difficult one." He later said his comment was in response to a post by Palestinian activist Nerdeen Kiswani, who had written "Finally NYC is coming to Islam. Dogs definitely have a place in society, just not as indoor pets." She said she had posted during a debate about picking up pet waste in New York City.

In response to Kiswani's post, Fine posted, "For context, this is the leader of one of the key mainstream Muslim groups that supported [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani," but he did not apologize.

Last July, Fine called Somali American Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar a "Muslim terrorist" after she had called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal."

According to his campaign website, Bilzerian supports ending all foreign aid, including to Israel, and pushes an antisemitic claim that Jewish special interest groups are running the country into the ground.

Bilzerian is among other far-right conservative voices running in Florida who have been critical of Israel, including James Fishback for governor and Jake Lang for Senate.

The issue of U.S. support for Israel is playing out in other races, including the Democratic primary in Florida's 25th District, where incumbent Rep. Jared Moskowitz is trying to fend off a challenge from progressive Oliver Larkin. Moskowitz has been a supporter of Israel, while Larkin has called for the U.S. to cut off aid.

title: Who is Byron Donalds? The Trump ally is favored to become Florida's next governor.
description: It’s been over three decades since the Sunshine State elected a Democratic governor, but polls suggest the MAGA favorite could be in for a tight race in November.
fullText:
In February 2025, President Trump made a surprising endorsement in the Florida governor's race. It wasn't who he chose, but when he decided to back them that was unexpected. The primary was still 18 months away and the man he endorsed hadn't even declared his candidacy yet.

Still, Trump's word carries so much weight in the Republican Party, particularly in his newly adopted home state, that Rep. Byron Donalds quickly became the frontrunner in the Florida GOP gubernatorial primary.

"Byron Donalds would be a truly Great and Powerful Governor for Florida and, should he decide to run, will have my Complete and Total Endorsement," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time. "RUN, BYRON, RUN!"

Donalds formally entered the race five days after Trump's post. Throughout his campaign, polls have shown him well ahead of the other Republican candidates. If he wins the GOP primary on Tuesday, he would also be the favorite to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is ineligible to run for a third term.

It has been more than three decades since Florida elected a Democrat as its governor, but some of the GOP's victories during that span have been extremely close. Republicans are counting on Donalds to keep their winning streak alive as he gears up for what polls suggest could be another close contest against likely Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who left the GOP during Trump's first presidential term.

Here's a guide to who Byron Donalds is, what he stands for and what his potential election might mean for America's third most populous state.

Donalds, 47, was born in New York City in 1978. He is of Jamaican and Panamanian heritage and was raised by his mother, describing himself as the "product of a single-parent household." Donalds grew up in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn before moving to Florida for college. He graduated from Florida State University in 2002 with a bachelor's degree in finance and marketing, and stayed in Florida to launch a career in the banking and insurance industries.

Donalds has said that his inspiration to go into politics came from anger over how Congress handled the aftermath of the 2008 financial collapse and the ensuing bank bailouts. A registered Democrat at the time, Donalds opted to switch parties and embraced the fiscally conservative worldview of the burgeoning tea party movement, which advocated for low taxes and reduced government spending.

"I got mad," Donalds said during a podcast interview earlier this month. "It pissed me off. That's how I got into politics and from there got involved in the Tea Party."

As a young Black man, Donalds stood out within a movement that was largely associated with older white voters. In 2012, he joined a crowded GOP primary for an open House seat, but finished fifth out of six candidates. In 2016, he was elected to the Florida state legislature.

He ran for Congress again in 2020 and, after being labeled a "Rising Star" by Trump following his primary win, was elected to the House of Representatives for the first time. He was the third Black Republican in history to represent Florida on Capitol Hill.

When he joined Congress, Donalds was part of a group of conservative lawmakers called the "Freedom Force," who were dedicated to countering the influence of progressive lawmakers like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. One of his first acts after being sworn in was to challenge the certification of the 2020 presidential election. He has repeatedly said that he does not believe that Joe Biden was a legitimately elected president.

In 2023, his name was raised as a potential House speaker multiple times during a drawn-out leadership crisis that ultimately led to Rep. Mike Johnson being elected speaker.

Donalds has been married to his wife, Erika Lees, since 2003. They have three children together. According to Donalds's first wife, Bisa Hall, Donalds began dating Lees while he and Hall were still married. Hall told WGCU News their marriage was not romantic and that they only wed to resolve what she described as a "residency issue" affecting her ability to attend college in Florida.

In 2022, Donalds was captured on camera having a heated argument with a woman inside a supermarket in Naples, Fla. The woman, Kelly Mason, who is currently a member of the Collier County School Board, filed a civil lawsuit over the incident in July, accusing him of assault. In a statement, Donalds's campaign called the lawsuit "baseless" and "politically motivated."

Donalds has closely aligned himself with Trump's MAGA policies. The words "Enact the Trump Agenda" appear in large bold letters at the top of the "issues" page of his campaign website.

He has endorsed Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, including arguing that undocumented immigrants facing deportation should not be entitled to due process under the law and criticizing the Supreme Court for striking down the president's attempt to revoke birthright citizenship.

Donalds is staunchly conservative on social issues. He supports placing strict limits on abortion access, wants to expand gun rights, has called for eliminating "woke ideology" in schools and supports restrictions on transgender rights, including barring transgender women and girls from women's sports. Donalds has also said he does not believe in man-made climate change.

If elected, he has pledged to block "sanctuary" jurisdictions that don't comply with federal immigration enforcement from receiving state funding, give parents more influence over their children's education and reform Florida's struggling property insurance industry.

The last time Florida elected a new governor with Trump in the White House was in the "blue wave" midterm cycle of 2018, when DeSantis narrowly defeated Democrat Andrew Gillum by less than half a percentage point. Though the national political environment appears to be swinging against the GOP again this year, polls have shown Donalds holding a steady lead of roughly five percentage points in head-to-head general election matchups.

title: In Florida, Wasserman Schultz sparks a debate over what representation means in diverse districts
description: Sporting red-white-and-blue sneakers and a matching bedazzled manicure ahead of Florida's primaries on Tuesday, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz smiles and tells voters she is “running for reelection to ...
fullText:
TAMARAC, Fla. (AP) — Sporting red-white-and-blue sneakers and a matching bedazzled manicure ahead of Florida's primaries on Tuesday, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz smiles and tells voters she is "running for reelection to Congress."

That's true — with a caveat. Wasserman Schultz is seeking her 12th term by running in a new district after Republicans scrambled the state's congressional map earlier this year.

The fallout pushed Wasserman Schultz, a former national party chair with powerful ties in Washington, to cross district lines from her Fort Lauderdale exurb and be the only white candidate against four Black candidates in an area of Broward County that has helped send Black Democrats to Congress since 1992. That's yielded an uncomfortable fight following the U.S. Supreme Court decision that gutted the Voting Rights Act provisions undergirding minority voting strength and effectively cleared Old Confederacy states, including Florida, to reshape House districts.

"For her to come in like this is just another Broward seat, it's a complete erasure of our history, our fight for Black access," said former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, 47, who resigned from the seat in April while facing an ethics investigation but now wants it back.

Another candidate, 27-year-old progressive organizer and substitute teacher Elijah Manley, said Republicans' redistricting ploy is not Wasserman Schultz's fault. But she "had other options," Manley added, including running in her new home district, which was gerrymandered to include the more conservative Gulf Coast.

"Instead, she stabbed us in the back, trying to take away Black representation," Manley said, pointing to Congressional Black Caucus warnings that it could lose more than a quarter of its 60-plus members this fall.

Wasserman Schultz, 59, is by far the best funded out of five Democratic candidates and benefits from Florida rules that do not require a majority to win primaries.

She argued that she can ably advocate for the whole region after representing wide swaths of Broward as a state and federal legislator across three decades. "I'm not air dropping myself into this district," she told The Associated Press. "I have represented diverse communities. I know how to tailor my service to them and represent a district more broadly."

President Donald Trump started pushing Republican-run states to redraw House boundaries last year to help preserve the party's fragile majority. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis responded with an effort that clusters southeast Florida Democrats together, intending to reduce five Democratic seats to three. Broward, the state's most Democratic county, situated between Miami-Dade and Palm Beach, now has just one presumed-Democratic district anchored in and around Fort Lauderdale.

Nationally, white lawmakers typically hold some of the 115-plus House seats where the voting-age population is majority non-white. Wasserman Schultz does it in her existing north Broward-Palm Beach district, which was drawn after the 2020 census to be 42% Hispanic, 18% Black and about 6% Asian American. White voters compose the remaining third.

But a white lawmaker is a rarity for majority or plurality Black districts, like the new Florida 20th. The district is 42% Black, 23% Hispanic and 4% Asian, the rest white. The Black share includes a large Caribbean population, most notably Haitian Americans.

Going into November, an Associated Press analysis found that Wasserman Schultz is the only white Democrat positioned to represent any of the remaining districts with a Black majority or plurality.

Cherfilus-McCormick said she can win, despite losing Black constituents she previously represented in Palm Beach County. She dismissed concerns over federal criminal charges accusing her of stealing $5 million in federal disaster funds. She has pleaded not guilty and has denied alleged violations of House rules.

The criminal case and redistricting fit together, she insisted, and "the people see what's going on — them trying to silence the only Haitian member of Congress and take away our voice."

Manley, though, was more circumspect about Wasserman Schultz's status as the favorite. He mused about upsetting the veteran congresswoman on Tuesday yet looked ahead to the 2028 elections, hoping Black Democrats rally around one candidate rather than four. The current field also includes former 2 Live Crew rapper Luther "Uncle Luke" Campbell and real estate broker and former local elected official Dale Holness.

Von Howard, a Black resident of Plantation, said the choice was wrenching. He declined to disclose his vote but said he wanted someone who "understands the totality of the district."

"If you're not of the people, and you just want this for the clout, in some instances, that could be a turnoff," the 47-year-old said.

Broward NAACP President Marsha Ellison was more direct, without endorsing any candidate.

"The whole mission was to take away Black power, so we don't have representation to understand our lived experience," she said. "That may not be important to Debbie, but it's certainly important to us."

Wasserman Schultz said she occasionally hears those concerns from voters. Her response is that "lived experience matters, but experience broadly matters" as well.

She notes her Appropriations Committee seat, which could be even more influential should Democrats win a House majority. She recalls programs impacting Black communities she helped create and fund since her first years in the Florida Legislature.

"I fight every single day to help improve the lived experience of the people that I represent," she said.

Wasserman Schultz also said she's worked to connect across race and culture in Broward. Because of her existing district makeup, "I spent six years learning Spanish," to converse with individuals and in town halls, news conferences and interviews broadcast on Spanish-language stations.

"Out of respect," she said, "anything I can do to inspire people's confidence that the person representing them understands them."

Several times outside of early voting sites, Black, white and Hispanic voters waved or stopped to talk to the congresswoman. Among them were Broward County sheriff's deputies who wanted photos and a trio of women who lamented they had been drawn into a new Republican-leaning district.

Yusdefs Delgado, a naturalized citizen from Colombia, told Wasserman Schultz that he enjoys her social media posts but wants to hear more about policy and less about the president.

"We know Trump sucks," he told her, smiling and confirming that he voted for her. "I don't agree with her on everything, but she's closest to where I am, and I trust her to try to do the right thing for us," Delgado explained later.

Cherfilus-McCormick and Manley said that's not enough given the environment after the Supreme Court decision, Trump's attacks on diversity initiatives and his push to rewrite how the U.S. tells its history on race and racism.

"We're not at a place in this country where we can be completely colorblind politically," Manley said. "We're just not."

Wasserman Schultz said the new district "is drawn in a way that the plurality population has the ability to elect the person of their choice" — language that alludes to the now-diminished Voting Rights Act. Voters, she said, can "consider all of the qualities that matter to them."

As for putting herself on the ballot again, she remained unapologetic.

"Trump and DeSantis did this to our community," she said, adding, "I'll be damned if I'm going to let them steal Broward's political power, de-unify us and prevent us from standing up for our community's values."
