A Microsoft exec was gunned down in the middle of the road. Prosecutors say it was an elaborate plot
description: Jared Bridegan, a father of four, was gunned down after dropping his twins off with his ex-wife in Florida. His ex-wife’s husband is now going on trial for murder.
fullText:
The young Microsoft executive had just dropped off his twins at his ex-wife's home in Jacksonville Beach on a warm, late-winter Florida evening. Towering live oaks draped with Spanish moss lined the neighborhood, casting long shadows across the pavement as the sun began to set.

He started driving home with his 2-year-old daughter in the backseat when he came upon a tire in the middle of the road. He stopped his car and got out to move it. But before he could get back behind the wheel, someone shot him dead in the street and fled.

Jared Bridegan, 33, had made the drive from Jacksonville Beach to his home in nearby St. Augustine countless times before. And that Wednesday in February 2022 had unfolded like any other: dinner with his toddler and twins, handing off the twins to their mother, and the evening drive home to his wife and baby.

But prosecutors say Bridegan's killer knew his routine, too, and had planted the tire to lure him out of the car. Jacksonville Beach Police Chief Paul Smith called it "a planned and targeted ambush and murder."

Multiple bullets pierced Bridegan's body and vehicle – one just inches from his toddler, Bexley, who was uninjured and crying, still strapped into her car seat, according to CNN affiliate WJXT, which cited prosecutors. Shell casings littered the dark residential street after the shooting.

Bridegan's body was left splayed in the street, with his car, wallet, wristwatch and other personal items untouched, according to police. Nothing appeared to have been taken.

Investigators say the incident was part of a monthslong murder-for-hire plot set in motion by Shanna Gardner, Bridegan's ex-wife, and her husband, Mario Fernandez Saldana, who goes on trial Monday.

Investigators have said Gardner was tired of sharing custody of the twins with Bridegan, CNN affiliate WJXT reported, citing detectives, and court documents say the former couple had been in a contentious custody battle for several years.

On the night of the killing, Gardner told police "the divorce was not amicable" between her and Bridegan, and they communicated only by text, according to WJXT. Police that night also spoke to Kirsten, Bridegan's widow, who said Gardner and Fernandez Saldana were the only people "who had ill will toward him," according to prosecutors' court docs, as reported by WJXT.

The State Attorney's Office declined to comment on the case ahead of opening statements Monday. But according to court documents, Gardner's father was willing to pay off Bridegan to get rid of him, WJXT reported. Prosecutors have also pointed to statements from a friend recounting Fernandez Saldana once telling her, "I've killed people before," and Gardner saying her husband could "take care of (Bridegan) and no one would ever know."

Police have said that's exactly what Fernandez Saldana tried to do in hiring a man to shoot and kill Bridegan.

After Bridegan was shot in the street, prosecutors have said, one person fled on foot and another fled in a vehicle, WJXT reported.

In early 2023, nearly a year after the shooting, investigators arrested the person they say pulled the trigger: 62-year-old Henry Tenon, who had rented a property from Fernandez Saldana.

Fernandez Saldana, now 38, is the first to stand trial in the case. He was arrested in Orlando in March 2023 on charges including first-degree murder and solicitation to commit a capital felony. He has pleaded not guilty, and CNN has reached out to his attorney for comment.

Tenon's arrest was a key break in the case, according to police.

"Our investigation has revealed a single link between Jared Bridegan and Henry Tenon," Melissa Nelson, Fourth Judicial Circuit state attorney, said. "That is Mario Fernandez Saldana."

Tenon was charged with conspiracy to commit murder, second-degree murder with a weapon, accessory after the fact to a capital felony and child abuse, Nelson said at the time.

GPS evidence released by prosecutors shows Tenon allegedly driving Bridegan's route twice in the month before the shooting, in what they called "a practice run of the homicide route," WJXT reported.

The affidavit in the case says investigators found three checks Fernandez Saldana wrote to Tenon in October 2022, CNN previously reported, and phone records show the men had more than 60 phone contacts with each other.

Fernandez Saldana "was integral to the solicitation, conspiracy, and murder of Bridegan," prosecutors said.

Tenon pleaded guilty only to second-degree murder with a weapon in March 2023, under a deal that required he testify against Fernandez Saldana and Gardner in exchange for dropped charges and a reduced sentencing range, WJXT reported.

In January 2025, however, Tenon backtracked, saying his testimony as part of the deal was "false." A judge granted Tenon's request to take back his guilty plea and proceed with a trial instead, with no objections from prosecutors.

At a bond hearing earlier this year, Fernandez Saldana's attorney said there was no proof his client's guilt was evident, CNN affiliate Action News Jax reported. Attorney Jesse Dreicer suggested Tenon made false statements and his confession to the shooting was coerced.

The defense then showed the court a police interview. In it, Fernandez Saldana says he was home at an hour the defense argues would have made it impossible for him to assist Tenon in the shooting.

Tenon's trial is scheduled for March 2027.

And five months after Fernandez Saldana's arrest, Gardner was also taken into custody. A grand jury indicted her on charges of first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit first-degree murder, solicitation to commit first-degree murder and child abuse related to the killing of her ex-husband.

Gardner has pleaded not guilty and is up next for trial, with a start date planned for early September.

"This investigation has uncovered the truth of Jared's murder. Henry Tenon did not act alone. Mario Fernandez did not plan alone," Nelson said in August 2023, after Gardner's arrest. "And Shanna Gardner's indictment acknowledges her central and key role in the cold, calculated and premeditated murder of Jared Bridegan."

title: Jack Whaley wins the U.S. Amateur title: Florida State fans react
description: Jack Whaley etched his name into Florida State golf history by winning the U.S. Amateur title. Here's how fans reacted.
fullText:
Jack Whaley etched his name into Florida State golf history by winning the 126th U.S. Amateur Championship on Sunday, with a 4-and-3 win over Stanford's Jay Leng Jr at Merion Golf Club in Pennsylvania.

Whaley battled both rainy conditions and some incredible golf from Leng to become the first Seminole in program history to earn the Havemeyer Trophy. He's just the third Englishman to win the prestigious amateur honor, and the first since current PGA Tour pro Matt Fitzpatrick in 2013.

With his father on the bag, Whaley navigated a 36-hole final day with precision and confidence. Down two strokes after the first 18 holes, Whaley drained putt after putt, including a run of four straight hole wins, in the final 18 to come back and hold off Leng for the championship.

Whaley won in front of FSU men's golf head coach Trey Jones, who flew up to watch the final day of action early Sunday morning. His victory earns him a spot in the 2027 Masters Tournament, British Open and US Open.

The win captured the attention of the Seminole faithful and golf fans around the globe. Here are a few reactions to Whaley's U.S. Amateur Championship.

title: Nearly 10 years after a Florida teen vanished in the middle of the night, detectives turn to psychics for help
description: Patrick Reeder’s 15-year-old daughter, Sophie, has been missing for just over nine years. Since then, the case has gone cold and there have been few developments, he said.
fullText:
Patrick Reeder's 15-year-old daughter, Sophie, has been missing for just over nine years. Since then, the case has gone cold and there have been few developments, he said.

Desperate for answers, Reeder is depending on detectives investigating his daughter's disappearance to crack the case.

But their latest investigative tool is not exactly what he had in mind.

"I just don't get it," Reeder told CNN. "A psychic?"

Since the teen vanished in the middle of the night after leaving her Fort Lauderdale, Florida, home, Sophie's case has garnered national attention and was featured on NBC's "Dateline: Missing in America" podcast last year. Sophie's story was also the subject of a 2021 episode of "In Pursuit with John Walsh."

With her disappearance still a mystery despite the national spotlight, the Fort Lauderdale Police Department has taken the rare step of consulting two psychic profilers, according to a department spokesperson.

"Traditionally, FLPD does not consult anyone outside of law enforcement on ongoing criminal cases," the spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. "However, in Sophie's case, our department is willing to try new and unique approaches for any chance at uncovering new information regarding her disappearance."

The unorthodox approach raises questions for the Reeder family about police's investigative strategy. Kirsten Milhorn, Reeder's sister, told CNN the move is "a misallocation of resources."

While there is no solid evidence that psychics can solve crimes, some law enforcement agencies use them when traditional leads run dry.

"Not everyone is going to be open to a psychic medium," said Alejandra Taborn, one of the psychic profilers working on Sophie's case. "But what I have found is even if they're not, what else do you have to lose?"

Before she disappeared, Sophie was a great kid with an artistic "flair," Reeder said, but she did deal with "some family issues" growing up.

"She's very interesting, very deep," Reeder said of his daughter, who also loved learning about the world, hair and makeup, religion and how things worked.

He never imagined she would vanish from his life on the night of May 19, 2017. Reeder said he spotted Sophie moseying around the house on her phone, so he told her to go to bed.

"It turns out she didn't go to bed," Reeder said. "She left."

Surveillance video from a home in her neighborhood, Citrus Isle, shows the teen walking on the sidewalk around 11:30 p.m. In a separate surveillance video, Sophie is seen walking along Davie Boulevard – a major road not far from her home – just after 2 a.m.

Her brown, curly hair pulled back into space buns, Sophie is seemingly alone on the desolate street, wearing headphones. At the time of her disappearance, the teen was about five feet tall and weighed approximately 100 pounds.

Records from Sophie's phone and Google account indicate her last known location was an apartment complex less than two miles from her house, according to a 2017 police affidavit and application for a search warrant filed in the case.

The complex was home to a then-37-year-old convicted felon named Leonard Jennings, who Fort Lauderdale police say is a "person of interest," not a suspect, in Sophie's case.

"FLPD believes Sophie had contact with [Jennings] on the night of her disappearance," a police spokesperson told CNN.

The affidavit shows the last phone call Sophie made was to Jennings' phone number at 3:07 a.m. that night, right as she arrived at the apartment complex.

After that call ended, Sophie's phone continued to ping from that location until 9:13 a.m., according to police records. The phone then stopped connecting to the cellular network, possibly turned off or disabled, the affidavit said.

What happened next has remained a persistent mystery.

Now, nearly a decade later, the department has taken a step — consulting psychics — that a police spokesperson admits is unusual and has raised the eyebrows of Sophie's loved ones. But Taborn, a Tampa-based psychic profiler and medium who assists law enforcement on cold cases, said she diligently carries out her job, including in Sophie's case, despite what others may think.

"This work is really important to me," Taborn told CNN. "It, like, lights my soul on fire."

Detectives first consulted Taborn earlier this summer, which involved a 90-minute virtual, introductory meeting, she said, noting she was paid by police.

"Any specific details and impressions that come through — that's how that consult goes," Taborn told CNN.

Since 2025, the department has consulted two psychics in Sophie's case, according to police. The Fort Lauderdale Police Department told CNN one psychic was paid $1,500 for a 90-day consulting period.

"Detectives are actively evaluating the information provided and determining if there's anything that may assist the investigation," the spokesperson added, declining to provide more details about what was discussed in the meeting.

Detectives spoke with another psychic who first reached out to Sophie's family before detectives followed up with them, police said, adding the psychic had offered services for free. The conversation prompted an investigation of a canal.

"We immediately began conducting an extensive search in the canal and surrounding area," the police spokesperson said, not revealing the location. "Unfortunately, this search yielded no results."

While skeptical, Reeder and Milhorn remain open to the process, even as doubts swirl.

"If that's something that actually bears fruit, and yeah, I'll jump on it," Reeder said. "But instead of that, there's a lot of other things they could do, you know, like a larger reward" than the $25,000 currently offered.

Skeptics say such psychic profilers do more harm than good by wasting police resources and exploiting grieving families. Among them is Benjamin Radford, a research fellow and investigator with the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry, a nonprofit organization that evaluates paranormal and fringe-science claims from a scientific viewpoint.

"Typically, what happens in these cases is that there'll be a missing persons case, and psychics, or self-proclaimed psychics, will sort of come out of the woodwork and offer information," Radford told CNN.

But based on his own investigations over 20 years, the track record of psychics finding missing persons is near zero, Radford said.

Still, Taborn believes her work can give law enforcement and families more information.

"Police are very intuitive themselves," said Taborn, who has developed a training program she said enables law enforcement to identify and strengthen their intuition.

Following a consultation, Taborn's process follows three steps, which she notes have not yet taken place in Sophie's case.

First, while wearing gloves, Taborn touches evidence or something connected to the case or the missing person — watching for signs or impressions, she said.

Then, Taborn said, she meets with the victim's family and assesses any information that comes through that may be relevant.

This step is unique to the family and could sometimes include specific details. "Anywhere from names, how they look, how they carry themselves," Taborn said.

The third step, Taborn said, involves going into the field with investigators and reading the energy of the environment.

While Radford said his goal is to hold psychics accountable, he doesn't believe they are all just out for profit.

"In my research, most of the people who claim to be psychics are sincere," Radford said. "Usually they're doing it because they sincerely want to help. Because there's a missing person and it tugs at your heartstrings."

Coping with the unknown has not always been easy for Reeder.

For many years after his daughter disappeared, any sense of normalcy vanished, too.

"I couldn't sleep in the bed," Reeder said. "I had to sleep on the couch, near the door, for like a couple years, just waiting for her to come home."

For loved ones of missing persons, that's not an unusual response to have, according to Dr. Dara DeLeon, a clinical psychologist based in Asheville, North Carolina, and a board member of "Sophie's Light," a nonprofit founded by Milhorn with the goal of developing an online safety curriculum for schools and children.

The grief Sophie's family has experienced is similar to post-traumatic stress, DeLeon notes, and feeling unheard or betrayed by law enforcement can only compound those emotions.

Reeder said he has experienced that feeling of betrayal firsthand.

"We tried so many times to get involved," he said, "and the detectives at Fort Lauderdale Police Department keep on shutting us down."

In response to a CNN request for comment, a police spokesperson said, "We are sad to hear this feedback from the family."

While the Reeder family continues to wait for answers — from psychics or elsewhere — Sophie's father has begun to make peace with the agonizing situation that has now prompted authorities to seek clarity from the beyond.

"I believe things happen for a reason," Reeder said. "You get put in situations and it builds you stronger for other things to help other people."

Anyone with information related to the disappearance of Sophie Reeder should call 954-828-6677 or email SophieTips@fortlauderdale.gov. Any credible information that leads to Sophie's recovery may be eligible for a reward of up to $25,000.

title: Pallister stuns Ledecky in Pan Pacs 800m free as two world records carry Douglass to gold
description: Australian Lani Pallister dealt US great Katie Ledecky her first 800m freestyle defeat in a major international meet on Saturday, beating her one-time idol at the Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California.Canadian Summer McIntosh did beat Ledecky in the 800m free at a minor domestic meeting in Florida in February of 2024.
fullText:
Australian Lani Pallister dealt US great Katie Ledecky her first 800m freestyle defeat in a major international meet on Saturday, beating her one-time idol at the Pan Pacific Championships in Irvine, California.

Pallister led wire-to-wire on the way to victory in 8min 06.10sec and Ledecky's desperate late charge wasn't enough as she finished second in 8:07.26.

It was a stunning result on the final day of Pan Pacs action that saw American Kate Douglass break the 50m freestyle world record twice on the way to gold and earn 200m breaststroke silver and medley relay gold as well.

Ledecky has dominated the 800m since she won Olympic gold in 2012 as a 15-year-old, winning 13 international golds since then. That includes four Olympic gold medals and seven world titles in the event.

Canadian Summer McIntosh did beat Ledecky in the 800m free at a minor domestic meeting in Florida in February of 2024.

But world record-holder Ledecky maintained her hold on the event with a razor-thin victory over Pallister and McIntosh in a World Championships thriller last year in Singapore, where Ledecky said her rule as younger swimmers began closing in was "I don't lose 800s."

Pallister, who claimed her first career win over Ledecky in the 400m free earlier this week before finishing second behind her in the 1,500m, showed that rule can be broken as the 29-year-old American looks to adding to her collection of nine Olympic gold medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The Australian punched the water in delight and got a hug across the lane rope from Ledecky.

"Katie is such a dominant force," said Pallister, who finished the week with gold in the 200, 400 and 800m free and the 4x200m free relay.

"Without her, we wouldn't have women's distance swimming in the place we're at at the moment.

"To be part of that story at the moment (it's) pretty much all because we get to chase Katie."

Douglass, meanwhile, firmly established herself as the one to chase in the 50m free, winning the final in a devastating 23.19sec.

That sliced three-tenths of a second off the world record of 23.49sec she set hours earlier and saw her finish a whopping 55-hundredths of a second ahead of US teammate Gretchen Walsh.

Walsh had set a world record of 23.55 on June 28 in Rome -- where she broke the world mark Douglass had set on June 19.

Australia's reigning world champion Meg Harris took bronze in 23.89.

Douglass returned less than half an hour later to claim silver in the 200m breaststroke won by Canadian Alexanne LePage in 2:21.73.

Douglass capped her night swimming the freestyle anchor leg for the US 4x100 medley relay team that took gold in 3:50.43, 4.66sec ahead of Australia.

Australian Jamie Jack won the men's 50m free in 21.35sec and Zac Stubblety-Cook rallied from fourth at the final turn to win the men's 200m breaststroke in 2:08.09 and give Australia another gold in the four-day meeting of top swimmers from non-European countries.

- More McIntosh disappointment -

Chinese Olympian Yu Yiting started the night with an upset of world record-holder Summer McIntosh in the 200m medley, leading most of the way and holding off the Canadian's charge on the final freestyle leg to win in 2:07.45.

McIntosh, the reigning world and Olympic champion, touched in 2:07.47.

It was another disappointment for McIntosh in a meet that included 400m medley gold but only silver in the 200m free and a failure to make the championship final in the 400m free.

Japan's Tomoyuki Matsushita completed a men's medley double with a 200m victory in 1:56.02.

Sam Short clocked an Australian record of 14:33.97 to add 1,500m freestyle to his 400m and 800m gold.

Short, who pulled off the same treble at the Commonwealth Games, finished 8.62sec in front of Japan's Kazushi Imafuku and said he was inspired by the world record of 14:26.79 set by Germany's Johannes Liebmann at the European Championships in Paris on Saturday.

American Bobby Finke, the two-time Olympic gold medallist whose world mark was broken by Liebmann, was third in 14:44.26.

title: Rashida Tlaib rally moved after Jewish-owned Florida venue cancels event, cites 'increased security concerns'
description: A Jewish-owned Fort Lauderdale venue canceled a rally set to headline Rashida Tlaib days before Florida's primary, citing security concerns.
fullText:
Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., an outspoken critic of Israel, was set to headline a rally in South Florida boosting three progressive Democratic candidates before the Jewish-owned venue hosting the event backed out a day before.

The Chomp the Oligarchy rally to support two U.S. House candidates and one Senate candidate was scheduled for Friday night at The Venue in Fort Lauderdale, just four days before Florida's primary election.

State Rep. Michael Gottlieb, a Democrat, posted Thursday morning calling the event "anti-Jew," while also accusing House candidates Elijah Manley and Oliver Larkin, along with state Rep. Angie Nixon, who is seeking the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, of being part of an "Anti-Israel and Anti-Zionism coalition."

Gottlieb then said Tlaib "has by far the deepest record of antisemitic allegations and is being brought here to help these candidates raise funds for their campaigns."

Jewish California Congressional Candidate Says Harassment From Gaza Agitators Went 'Beyond Free Speech'

After Gottlieb's post, The Venue posted a statement Thursday night indicating that the event was canceled, citing "increased security concerns."

The statement did not mention Tlaib by name but said management pulled out after becoming aware of the "full scope" of the event and reviewing promotional materials.

"Due to the increased security concerns as well as the welfare of attendees and staff, the decision was then made that the event would not proceed at our property," the statement said. "The Venue Fort Lauderdale is Jewish-owned and operated, and our values and commitment to the Jewish community are deeply important to us."

Fox News Digital reached out to The Venue for additional comment. Tlaib's representatives did not immediately return a request for comment.

Democrats Split Over Tlaib's Lebanon Measure As Republicans Seize On Hezbollah Omission

Prior to the event being canceled, The Venue reached out to Gottlieb, asking him to take down his post, something he refused to do, The New York Times reported.

Cameron Driggers, a lead organizer for the rally, told the Times The Venue reached out to the rally organizers saying it would only host the event if Tlaib was uninvited, but the organizers refused.

Manley, who has been endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, is facing off against Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla., while Larkin, a self-identified DSA member, is challenging incumbent Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.

Nixon is running against Alexander Vindman, a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel known for testifying during President Donald Trump's first impeachment inquiry.

Jeffries Declines To Back Wasserman Schultz As Black Leaders Revolt Over District Switch

The Chomp the Oligarchy event's organizers said on Instagram that they "will not be silenced by racist right-wing agitators and conservative Democrats," adding that they will "keep fighting to deliver for working-class Floridians."

The rally ended up taking place at an alternate outdoor location reportedly with about 300 supporters in attendance.

In his speech, Larkin addressed the tumult surrounding the event.

"What we've seen in the last 36 hours is a mobilization campaign to try to intimidate and harass us with a campaign of Islamophobia. A campaign that seeks to excuse AIPAC's corrupting influence over our elections," Larkin said to a chorus of boos from the crowd.

Tlaib also appeared at the rally as planned, introducing Nixon before she delivered her remarks.

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital Wednesday "it's no coincidence" Tlaib would be appearing at an event supporting candidates seeking to defeat Jewish Democrats.

Tlaib, the first Palestinian American woman in Congress, has faced bipartisan criticism for her comments on Israel and Jewish people. The Michigan congresswoman has denied accusations of antisemitism.

Congress censured Tlaib in 2023 for her embrace of the slogan "from the river to the sea," which she says is an "aspirational call for freedom, human rights, and peaceful coexistence" from Palestinians. Many Jews view the slogan as a veiled call for genocide against Israelis.

title: AD Alford: ‘Excitement Around Seminoles Football is High’
description: Florida State athletic director Michael Alford was interviewed on the ACC Huddle: Florida State Road Trip. He offered some insights into how Florida State is competing with its peers in the arena of college athletics.
fullText:
For thelast seven years, Florida State athletic director Michael Alford has crisscrossedthe southeastern portion of the United States championing his university toboosters, parents and potential student athletes.

His mission: raise funds andrecruit talent to Florida State.

On the ACCHuddle-Florida State Road Trip show, Alford was interviewed, and he offeredsome insights into the "business" end of college football.

"When I arrivedsix, seven years ago, Florida State was not up to par to what our peers were,and we had to invest in the resources," said Alford. "Offering a holistic view,we have a top 25 public education we can offer, now we got these facilities.And, when you come and train mind, body and soul, then you have to invest in thetalent acquisition. We are doing that at a high level and giving them the bestof both worlds in coming to Florida State. It really represents what FloridaState is about, the class of this university, the community and our program."

So far,this year has been the most successful year of fundraising for Florida Stateboosters, bringing in a record-setting $106 million. Alford and his departmentare committed to providing all that is necessary to help his teams be competitive,and ultimately win.

"You haveto invest and give them the resources," said Alford. "In the last severalyears, we've done over $550 million in renovations. We are giving them theresources, now they got to go produce."

Unfortunately,that production has not materialized on the gridiron for the Seminoles. 17losses in their last 24 games is not a good return on investment, by anymeasure. But as the new season approaches, Alford said. "Excitement around thisteam is high."

Astraining camp draws to a close and the week zero game with New Mexico State is uponus, fans and the media could see coach Mike Norvell lead a different FloridaState team out of the tunnel at Doak Campbell Stadium.

Men with adesire to be better versions of themselves, to play together as a band ofbrothers, forged in blood, sweat and tears. They endured the blistering summerheat to transform themselves into warriors in search of gridiron glory, notonly for themselves, but for a grateful fan base.

Players flirtedwith the transfer portal, but changed their minds and returned because they believedin their development within the Seminoles program. Coaches stayed, trained theirplayers hard over the summer leading up to fall camp. Camp is where boys becomemen, hardened by the daily grind, chipping away at the player he was and becominga player with a different mindset.

Lastseason, four of Florida State's losses were by eight points or fewer. Apositive play here or there would have meant the difference between a 5-7 losingseason, and a respectable 9-3 season.

September will be the telling point this season. SMU and Alabama, bothranked in the preseason top 25, dot the schedule right out of the gate. Couldthere be chaos in leadership on the sidelines before the calendar changes toOctober? Norvell believes the Seminoles are primed to do something special thisseason.

Saturdaysin the fall are where the investment in facilities and talent pays dividends. Alfordand the university have receipts. Norvell is currently in default and if theSeminoles do not produce on the field in the form of wins, then Alford willhave no choice but to foreclose on Norvell's career at Florida State.

title: Former Gator Bradley Beal remains with Clippers after new contract
description: After waiting throughout most of the free agency period, former Florida basketball guard Bradley Beal re-signs with the Los Angeles Clippers.
fullText:
Former Florida basketball guard Bradley Beal has agreed to a two-year, $13.2 million deal to return to the LA Clippers, ESPN reports. The deal includes a player option in the second season.

After declining his $5.6 million player option, Beal spent the past month exploring his options in free agency, including interest from the Miami Heat, before ultimately deciding to remain with the Clippers.

Beal's decision to opt out allowed him to test his value on the open market while also giving Los Angeles additional flexibility to explore its roster options. In the end, the Clippers opted to retain Beal with a significant raise on a new two-year contract.

Beal's first season with the Clippers did not go as planned, as he only appeared in six games, but the new contract allows him to reset heading into his 15th NBA season. Beal, a three-time NBA All-Star, will look to stay healthy and recapture the form that made him one of the league's premier scoring guards during his time with the Washington Wizards.

With Los Angeles transitioning toward a younger roster, Beal's experience could provide valuable leadership while he looks to carve out a meaningful role on the second unit. If he can return to form, the former Gator could prove to be an important piece for the Clippers over the next two seasons.

title: Mission Improbable: A onetime Republican is trying to prove Democrats can win in Florida
description: Cyn Doyle is a self-described political cynic.  As the crowd in the clubhouse of a manufactured home community for seniors jeered the mention of the contrarian Pennsylvania Democratic senator, Jolly, ...
fullText:
LEESBURG, Fla. (AP) — Cyn Doyle is a self-described political cynic. So when David Jolly, the Republican-turned-independent who is now running for Florida governor as a Democrat, swung through this town dotted by lakes and Spanish moss, she had doubts.

"How can you assure us," the 71-year-old pressed, "that you won't become another John Fetterman?"

As the crowd in the clubhouse of a manufactured home community for seniors jeered the mention of the contrarian Pennsylvania Democratic senator, Jolly, who once critiqued politicians as an MSNBC pundit, made the case for himself.

"Change is part of my journey," he responded. "What I can tell you is that the values I speak of — that the economy should work, that government can do a little bit to improve our lives and that everyone should have the right to be protected — those are the guideposts for how I'll serve as governor."

Doyle, an independent who said she's a registered Democrat mostly to participate in primaries, left impressed.

"I believe him," she said. "I don't believe many."

Florida spent a generation as America's prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.

Jolly is bent on proving those days aren't over.

In the course of a single day last weekend, he rallied a chandeliered ballroom in The Villages, a wealthy Republican-leaning retirement community. Then it was off to the fluorescent lights of the Leesburg clubhouse before ending with a rousing speech to Democrats in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, which backed a Republican presidential candidate for the first time in 20 years in 2024.

President Donald Trump's rise has coincided with a Democratic collapse in Florida. He won here three times, with ever-expanding margins. The 19-percentage-point win by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis in 2022 cemented a GOP supermajority in the legislature.

Jolly's path to victory could be blocked by both math and money in his likely race against Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-backed candidate in Tuesday's Republican primary. Donalds, who would be Florida's first Black governor, has raised more than $100 million compared to Jolly's $10 million.

Donalds has cast Jolly as an out-of-touch liberal, blanketing the state this week with an ad featuring Jolly referring to "gender-affirming care" and backing communities painting rainbow crosswalks to show support for LGBTQ people. Jolly countered that Donalds is ignoring pressing economic issues.

In an interview over an Outback Steakhouse lunch while his wife and two young children busied themselves with coloring, Jolly acknowledged "there's not going to be the political will" to reverse the state's ban on transgender girls and women participating on female teams at public schools and universities.

He said he didn't think governors should decide who plays in what sports even as he described himself as a "girl dad" and noted "I don't think we should have biologically born men playing in competitive sports."

"But look," he added, "if a 10- or 12-year-old soccer league in the community has a coed team, I don't think the governor should be throwing a flag on the field."

For all the headwinds confronting Jolly, Republicans may encounter their own turbulence.

The culture wars that have raged under DeSantis, including a feud with Disney and fights over gender and sexual orientation, have left some exhausted. Karen Kuhn, a 72-year-old resident at The Villages, described herself as in "despair."

Democrats have won a string of special elections from Miami to Palm Beach and Tampa, adding to their optimism. Former GOP Rep. Carlos Curbelo said Latinos who voted for Trump in 2024 might not support Republicans again, in part because of the administration's immigration enforcement tactics.

"I definitely can see a scenario where it's a closer race, where it's a competitive race," said Curbelo, who narrowly lost his reelection bid in 2018, the last wave election year for Democrats.

Jolly is telling that to any Democrat who will listen, including those with potential presidential ambitions such as Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois, Gavin Newsom of California, Andy Beshear of Kentucky and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. If Florida can change, he argues, the national political landscape would change with it.

"All of a sudden the road to the White House looks dramatically different," Jolly said. "It reshapes the House of Representatives. The structural change from winning Florida is a generational opportunity for Democrats."

It's a point echoed by other Democrats, including state Rep. Emily Gregory, who flipped the Palm Beach district home to Trump's Mar-a-Lago.

"To abandon Florida was deeply, deeply unwise," she said. "I hope that investment is coming back because it is a purple state and I feel very confident going into November."

Nikki Fried, the Florida Democratic Party chair, acknowledged "the bottom fell out" for Democrats. She has spent the past several years rebuilding the operation. Democrats charged with winning back state legislative and congressional seats are prioritizing some Florida races this year.

But Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association, isn't making a financial commitment yet.

"David's working really hard," he said in an interview. "He's a good candidate, and we're watching it closely."

Donalds' campaign remains confident. His communications director, Gates McGavick, said: "Florida voters will reject radical liberal David Jolly because he will make life more expensive."

Jolly is an unlikely figure cajoling Democrats to think about their future.

He first gained national attention in 2014 as the GOP winner of a Tampa Bay congressional seat that was seen as a bellwether. In a Democratic Party that emphasizes diversity, Jolly regularly refers to himself as a "53-year-old white former Republican with salt-and-pepper hair." His time in Congress runs counter to voters elevating fresher voices this year.

During stump speeches, he says he was a "Bush 41" Republican. He left the GOP in 2018, spending several years as an independent before registering as a Democrat in 2025.

Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings, who challenged Jolly until suspending his campaign in June and announcing he had prostate cancer, acknowledged Florida Democrats have to appeal to independents. But he also said "people don't want a chameleon."

"That's the big challenge that he's had, is convincing people that he has stepped away from the Republican policies," Demings said.

Sylvia Rieger, a 70-year-old resident at The Villages, said Jolly's evolution showed "moxie."

Steven Slyter, an 81-year-old retired handwriting expert, said it was "courageous" for Jolly to leave his party. "He made a decision about what he stands for," Slyter said. "I like that."

Florida's last Democratic candidate for governor, Charlie Crist, was also a former Republican. After his drubbing by DeSantis, several Democrats said Jolly was campaigning more effectively.

Facing minimal primary competition, Jolly has largely avoided debates over the party's ideological future. He's won support from progressives including Rep. Maxwell Frost while shoring up his centrist credentials by picking former Rep. Gwen Graham, the daughter of longtime Sen. Bob Graham, as his running mate.

Some Jolly supporters are hoping that his poly-party background will be an asset.

Jeff Adelman is running for a nonpartisan seat on the Coral Springs City Commission in Broward County. As he left a recent meeting of the Coral Springs Parkland Democratic Club, he described Jolly as a potentially unique fit for the state.

"We live in Florida," he said. "I don't think you're going to get somebody like Bernie Sanders to run for governor in the state of Florida."

title: Tlaib under fire for working to unseat two Jewish House Democrats in Florida: 'No coincidence'
description: Rashida Tlaib is rallying in Fort Lauderdale to back socialists challenging Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz in their primaries.
fullText:
Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., is being criticized by Florida's lone Jewish Republican in Congress as she works to unseat two fellow House Democrats.

Tlaib is appearing at a rally in Fort Lauderdale Friday held by left-wing groups in support of three congressional candidates, according to a flier posted on Instagram, including two socialists running to unseat Reps. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., and Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla.

"I think that it's no coincidence that she's coming to target two of the remaining Jewish Democrats," Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital.

Jeffries Declines To Back Wasserman Schultz As Black Leaders Revolt Over District Switch

"It won't be well received in Florida," he continued. "How it's received in a Democratic primary — look, the Democrats are lost. But I'm going to hope that Florida Democrats are smarter than national Democrats because the Jew hatred side of the Democratic Party is not good for America."

Tlaib has been a power player on the far left so far this election cycle as candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) dominate establishment Democrats in key elections across the country.

But DSA-linked candidates have also been accused of criticism against Israel that approaches antisemitism, according to the group's opponents, while being sympathetic to terror groups like Hamas.

Tlaib, the first Palestinian American woman in Congress, has faced bipartisan criticism for her comments on Israel and Jewish people. The Michigan congresswoman has denied accusations of antisemitism.

Former Bernie Sanders Official Accuses Senator Of Pushing Most Antisemitic Candidates 'In A Generation'

But Fine said Tlaib was a "vocal supporter of Hamas" and said the far left was making Jews in America feel unsafe.

"I think the Democratic Party is lost, and I think it's dangerous. I don't know that it's lost and dangerous in Fort Lauderdale or Florida, but nationally, the kinds of people that the Democrats are nominating, these are people who do not love America," Fine said of the far-left surge.

"They hate it. They are here to destroy it, and no one embodies that better than Rashida Tlaib."

DSA-linked candidates have already toppled House Democrats in New York, Colorado and Michigan. Also in Michigan, socialist politician Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens for the party's nomination for Senate.

Dems' Leftward Lurch Gets Legs As El-sayed's Michigan Senate Victory Sparks Party Debate

Tlaib campaigned with El-Sayed and other DSA candidates across the U.S.

Friday's rally is called Chomp the Oligarchy and is being hosted by progressive groups like Gen Z For Change and Florida Youth Justice Coalition.

Moskowitz and Wasserman Schultz's campaigns did not respond to requests for comment on Tlaib's appearance. Tlaib's campaign did not respond to a request for comment on Fine's remarks.

Tlaib and other Democrats have previously accused Fine of anti-Muslim racism.

Moskowitz, who represents Florida's 23rd Congressional District, is running for re-election in the 25th Congressional District, which was recently redrawn to give Republicans a better shot in the general race.

Wasserman Schultz is running in the newly redrawn 20th Congressional District, a majority-Black district that leans heavily Democratic, sparking backlash for potentially impacting the area's historically Black representation.

title: Florida deputy killed ex-girlfriend over a TV, then himself, sheriff says
description: Deputy Troy Savetz waited outside his ex-girlfriend's home with a gun, angry over a TV set, before abducting her as her children called 911 from inside.
fullText:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A Florida sheriff's deputy, honored multiple times for his bravery, dedication and compassion, killed a former girlfriend and then himself Monday after an argument over a television.

The victim was identified by friends as Mandy Fackler, who leaves behind two children, 12 and 9, Fox Tampa reported.

Deputy Troy Savetz had been with the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office for 14 years and was a member of the marine unit.

He and the victim had an "on-again-off-again, tumultuous relationship," Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri said in a news conference.

Missouri Mom Of 5 Fatally Shot While Buying Slushies With Children; Police Search For Gunman

Savetz, 47, was waiting outside Fackler's home when she and her children returned from a day at the beach at about 5:30 p.m. He brandished a gun and was angry about "wanting his TV set back," Gualtieri said.

When the victim tried to call 911, Savetz took her phone. That's when she told her two children to go inside.

They did as they were told. And they never saw her again.

The children were "extremely brave," calling 911 and giving dispatchers everything needed to identify the suspect, Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco told reporters.

When authorities arrived at the home, they saw the mother's vehicle with the door wide open, and they found her phone, Nocco said.

"At that point, they realize that she's no longer there" at the residence, he said.

Officers sprang into action using K-9 teams, drones and aviation units, searching for the vehicle Savetz was driving when he carried the victim away, Nocco said.

About 90 minutes after the altercation began, authorities found the vehicle in nearby Spring Hill. Officers approached with a drone and saw two people inside.

When they reached the car on foot, they found Savetz and his victim dead.

"We're not sure when and at what point" he killed her and himself, Nocco said.

The children, now with their biological father, were unharmed in the incident.

Dispatch Audio Released In Michigan Family Murder-suicide As Troubled Family's Secrets Emerge

They "should be starting off this week getting ready for school," Nocco said. Instead, they're "starting off this week getting ready for a sad life without their mother."

He praised the children for their bravery and obedience at such a critical moment.

"I know eventually there's going to be a point in your life where you're going to go back and listen to all the videos and read all the reports," Nocco said.

"So please hear this directly from us: We listened to that 911 tape, and we know that your mother said to go inside to save your lives and to call 911. You did exactly what your mom asked you to do.

"Know this: Your mom is looking down from heaven, and she's so proud of you two … So know that you two did the right thing."

Nocco said officers were "amazed" by the children's "calmness." The information they provided allowed for the fastest possible response.

"So we're so proud of you, and I know your mom is. But know [that] this entire community is praying for you."

Off-duty Trooper And Armed Citizen Hailed As Heroes After Returning Fire On In-n-out Gunman

Before this, Savetz had earned accolades for his behavior while wearing the badge. In 2014, he was honored by the sheriff's office for his "heroic action" in saving the life of a 24-year-old man, stopping him from jumping off a bridge in Pinellas County.

That earned him attention from the Tampa Bay Rays baseball team, who called him "Our Everyday MVP" in a June 2015 social media post. Wearing his green uniform, Savetz was honored by receiving the opportunity to throw out a ceremonial first pitch.

He was hailed a "hero" at local fundraisers and by radio stations.

In 2018, the sheriff's office shared a social media post about how Savetz had adopted a pot-bellied pig he found while on duty. That year, he and Maple, as she became known, went on to be named ambassadors for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals in Tampa Bay.

But the "inexcusable" behavior of Savetz immediately ended his identity as a law enforcement officer, Gualtieri said.

"The moment this individual committed a crime, he was no longer a law enforcement officer. He was a criminal."

title: Florida football coach Jon Sumrall discusses QB competition, WR Dallas Wilson status
description: Florida coach Jon Sumrall talks QB competition, managing injuries and offensive line as UF competes first weekend of fall camp.
fullText:
Though the first fall practices of fall camp, Florida football coach Jon Sumrall has been pleased with the effort and intensity on both sides of the ball.

"The intent of our guys has been good," Sumrall said. "There's been a lot of improvement, you know, certain guys are elevating. It's been fun to see some guys take steps forward."

The Florida Gators will practice in full pads for the first time on Tuesday, August 11 and hold their first intra-squad scrimmage on Saturday, August 15.

"We still need more out of certain guys as well. but like where we're at in a lot of ways," Sumrall said.

Sumrall, hired from Tulane last Nov. 30, is conducting his first fall camp in preparation for UF's season opener against Florida Atlantic on Sept. 5 at The Swamp (7:45 p.m.). He said he intends to play "a lot of guys" in the opener to get a feel for how they handle game situations.

"You can look at the teams I've had, game one where it's been non conference we've played more people then we'll play all year regardless of what the matchup is," Sumrall said. "We played Northwestern last year, game one, which is a Big Ten school, when I was at Tulane, and we played a ton of people in game one. I'm trying to figure out who our team is. I've got a decent idea in practice, but you don't really know who you got and who you are until you go play somebody else."

Here's what else Sumrall said following the first weekend in fall camp:

Sumrall said wide receiver Dallas Wilson working out on the JUGS machines on Friday, August 7, and not taking part in live drills was the result of a load management issue. Wilson dealt with a broken foot that limited him to four games last season and sidelined him for parts of spring practices

"We had a yardage for Wednesday's practice we wanted, a yardage for Thursday's practice we wanted, and then a de-load day for Friday's practice." Sumrall said. "He still went about 4,000 yards on Friday, he practiced, we cut back a lot of the individual reps and scaled back certain things he did to make sure he still got the right number of team reps. And then Saturday he was full-go, didn't miss anything."

When healthy, the 6-foot-3, 212-pound Wilson displayed star potential as a true freshman last season, catching 12 passes for 174 yards and 3 TDs in four games.

"Dallas is a unique case because return to play for him," Sumrall said. "I want to see him play on Saturdays against other people. He's obviously a known player in some regards, but does not have a lot of time on task. So while we all know how talented he is, there's still a ton of development left with Dallas as a player to be a polished route-runner and be refined."

Sumrall said senior defensive end Kamran James, a returning starter who tied a team-high with 3.5 sacks last season, is dealing with a "soft tissue" injury that he doesn't anticipate being serious.

As for other health updates, Sumrall said safety Kaiden Hall, tight end Jaylen Jordon, running back Duke Clark, wide receiver Marquez Daniel and cornerback CJ Bronaugh also have been limited in camp with soft tissue injuries. Running back Kelvin Jimenez is out for the "foreseeable future" with a contact injury, while tight end Evan Chieca is out for at least a week. Freshman defensive lineman Kendall Guervil re-aggravated a knee issue and is out.

Sumrall was asked his thoughts on how Aaron Philo and Tramell Jones Jr. have developed a bond off the field despite competing for the starting quarterback job. He compared it to a recent video Tim Tebow posted about wanting to beat out Chris Leak as a freshman, while building Leak up at the same time.

"I want our quarterback room to be motivated by other people's success, not intimidated," Sumrall said. "Somebody will go out and take the ball in game one, and I expect the guy who does to still be humble about his approach and work his tail off, and the guy who doesn't, I expect him to know, 'Hey I'm a play away from being put in the game', and prepare like a starter because you never know when your opportunity is coming.' "

Sumrall said that decision could stretch beyond the start of the 2026 sason.

"Are we ready to go name a starter today? No," Sumrall said. "We may not name one. You guys may go into the game, and you'll probably do your due diligence and find out who's taking reps with the ones the week of the first game, but I might not come out and make some formal announcement of who QB1 is. We're just probably not doing that. We're going figure out who to win a game with each week. That's our goal."

As for the offensive line, Sumrall said he's noticed "growth" through the first four practices of fall camp.

"The competition has been good," Sumrall said. "Still a lot of movement in nature in regard to like, Bryce Lovett may play some guard and some tackle, and then you might see one guy go with the ones in a rack and with the twos, so it's still not settled to where it's like a cohesive group."

As for the tackles, Sumrall mentioned Emeka Ugorji and Eagan Boyer as candidates to start on the left side and Lovett and Caden Jones as candidates to start on the right side. Fletcher Westphal, coming off offseason wrist surgery, could also work his way back to competing for either starting tackle spot.

"I'm not trying to project what's going to happen game one or game two, but I would say you will probably see us try to play several guys to see who they are, and whoever rolls out first is going to be who we felt has earned to go out first," Sumrall said. "We need to get several guys reps to create competitive depth."

title: Who can shake the depth chart in 'move week' for FSU football?
description: Florida State enters a critical move week as coach Mike Norvell works to finalize the depth chart before kickoff.
fullText:
After two weeks of preseason camp and a pair of scrimmages, Florida State football enters "move week" with spots on the depth chart up for grabs.

Head coach Mike Norvell said as much after the Seminoles' second scrimmage inside Doak Campbell Stadium on Sunday, Aug. 9. There are two weeks left in preseason camp before the program enters game week preparation for New Mexico State, and the coaching staff is working on finalizing position groups.

"Excited to jump into this week and continue to get better. This is going to be a big move week for us," Norvell said in a Zoom after the scrimmage. "We are starting to see who's emerging within the depth chart and really working to finalize some of those personnel groupings as we get ready for game prep here the following week."

There are a few roles and positions where players have already solidified their spots on the depth chart. Ashton Daniels is the starting quarterback, both Duce Robinson and Micahi Danzy are the top two receivers, and Ja'Bril Rawls and Ashlynd Barker are stars in the secondary.

So what positions are up for grabs heading into "move week" for the Seminoles? Let's take a look.

While Robinson and Danzy have had their names penciled in as the top two receivers since the final whistle of the 2025 season, the third receiver role remains a question.

A player that has made strides toward earning that role is true freshman Jasen Lopez. He's been one of the most heavily praised players in the preseason, and Norvell said he's earning his opportunities.

"He's still got plenty of things to be able to work on, plenty of things to grow in. But the mentality is one thing I do appreciate with him," Norvell said. "We're challenging him, asking him to do a lot of different things ... but he's definitely answered the call in a lot of ways."

It's not just Lopez in contention, though he seems to be the frontrunner, as Jayvan Boggs, Devin Carter, Tae'Shaun Gelsey and Teriq Mallory are also in play.

Carter had a big spring as a true freshman, and that's put him into a position to earn reps early on, even if he doesn't start. Boggs was a starter last season as a freshman, but he battled injuries, which have lingered into his sophomore season. If healthy, he's a dynamic route runner who could start, but he's being pushed by Lopez.

Both Gelsey and Mallory are in their second season and have developed after limited appearances as freshmen. A push for the starting spot is possible, though both players are likely going to start the year as backups. However, a big week of practice could open some eyes.

Rawls and Barker are locked in as starters at cornerback and safety, respectively, but what about the rest of the secondary?

Starting at corner, Norvell mentioned the battle for the second corner role after the scrimmage. For the week ahead, all of Nehemiah Chandler, Quindarrius Jones, Charles Lester III and Ricky Knight will be jostling for a chance to move their names up the depth chart.

"I think it's very competitive right now," Norvell said. "Q[uindarrius Jones] has been really good. You see Nehemiah Chandler, Charles Lester had a really nice pick tonight. A guy that we challenged, Ricky Knight. Who's going to emerge as one of those guys that can be counted on?"

Chandler transferred into the program after a standout season at South Alabama that landed him All-Sun Belt first team honors. He had 31 total tackles, two interceptions and 13 pass breakups and should see significant play time this season.

Q. Jones is a veteran in the room and has battled injury. Now healthy, he's impressed in the preseason and might be in line to start alongside Rawls in his senior season. Both Lester and Knight have yet to make good on their promise as highly touted recruits; could this week be an opportunity to change that? It'll be something we follow.

Linebacker is one of the key positions for the Seminoles in 2026. It's a key cog to Tony White's 3-3-5 scheme, and one that is likely to be anchored by Chris Jones. But who lines up with him could be identified this week.

The room has been hampered by injury with Mikai Gbayor and freshman sensation Izayia Williams both missing time, but if healthy, they could be the two starters with C. Jones. If they aren't healthy, where does that put the linebackers?

Returning veterans Caleb LaVallee, Omar Graham Jr. and Blake Nichelson are all options, and players who could jump up the depth chart with a strong week of practice.

"I think Omar Graham's playing really, really good ball. You're seeing guys like Blake Nicholson, Caleb LaVallee, that have been here. I think everybody's talked about Chris Jones. He's definitely been a force," Norvell said. "He's the guy that you really like to see. Izayia Williams, he was out tonight, but expecting him to get back in action here in this next week or so. A guy that I think is a young player who is going to have an opportunity to impact."

Arguably the most critical piece of any success for FSU this season is the offensive line. Protecting Daniels and allowing him to get the ball to playmakers, or open up gaps for the ground game, will be crucial.

There are some solidified starters, with Bradyn Welch-Joiner at center and Xavier Chaplin as one of the tackles. Nate Pabst, André Otto and Chimdia Nwaiwu are among the other players who can fill out the offensive line.

Is that set? It doesn't seem so, but this week is the chance for the trenches to be solidified as the first week of the season is quickly approaching.

title: Florida's Jon Sumrall looking to end his big-game woes this season

fullText:
CBS Sports examined every Power Four coach's career record against teams ranked in the AP Top 25, and at 2-7, Jon Sumrall sits near the bottom of the SEC. While at Troy, he lost to No. 21 Ole Miss in 2022 and No. 15 Kansas State in 2023, but beat No. 18 UTSA in the 2022 Cure Bowl. At Tulane, the head coach managed to upend No. 22 Memphis in 2025.

title: Passengers evacuated after Delta flight returns to Atlanta due to report of fumes in the flight deck, airline says
description: A Florida-bound Delta flight on Saturday returned to Atlanta and evacuated passengers on slides after reports of smoke in the cockpit.
fullText:
A Florida-bound Delta flight on Saturday returned to Atlanta and evacuated passengers on slides after reports of smoke in the cockpit.

"Delta 2204, change of plans. We now have smoke in the back, and we need to deplane immediately," according to air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com.

"The flight crew followed procedures to return to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport after reports of fumes in the flight deck," Delta Air Lines said in a statement.

"A slide evacuation occurred on a taxiway … Safety is paramount at Delta, and we apologize to our customers for their experience."

Flight 2204 from Atlanta to Orlando was carrying 199 passengers and six crew members, according to Delta. Passengers and crew on the Boeing 757 evacuated via slides on the taxiway and returned to the terminal on a bus. The flight departed at 7:23 a.m., according to flight tracking site FlightAware.

title: Florida business owners allegedly scattered 1,500 mothballs on beach to send endangered birds packing
description: Two St. Pete Beach business owners allegedly spread 1,500 toxic mothballs on sand to stop black skimmers from nesting and are facing felony charges.
fullText:
Two Florida business owners have been charged with third-degree felonies after allegedly spreading about 1,500 "toxic" mothballs across a beach in hopes of keeping an "imperiled" bird species from nesting there.

If convicted, they could each face up to five years in prison, fines of up to $5,000 and up to five years of probation.

The problem started in late April when beachgoers noticed mothballs on the white, sugary sand on St. Pete Beach in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and bird-loving volunteers from the Audubon Society mobilized. They plucked about 1,000 of the small, white orbs from the sand behind the Plaza Beach Hotel.

Massachusetts Homeowners Stunned After Town Warns July 4 Flags Threaten Endangered Birds

Then 500 more appeared overnight.

The smelly balls containing pesticides dotted an area where endangered shorebirds known as black skimmers were "attempting to establish a nesting colony," FWC officials said at a news conference. Their placement also meant other wildlife and children "could easily come in contact with them."

It quickly became clear that someone might be targeting the birds, they said.

So FWC investigators flew into action.

The discovery of the mothballs ruffled feathers in the community.

There was "a lot of public outcry," expressing concern for the birds, while investigators tried to locate the source of the mothballs, FWC officials said.

Law enforcement served search warrants, combed through "terabytes" of data and eventually seized cellphones to try to locate the individuals behind the caper.

That work led them to Christopher Monroe, owner and manager of Chris's Beachside Bar, and Robert Czyszczon, owner of the Plaza Beach Hotel, FWC officials said.

Out of fear of lost revenue, the two allegedly hatched a plan to use mothballs to deter birds from congregating on the beach behind their businesses, authorities said.

Through video surveillance and receipt records, investigators found that Czyszczon spent about $60 buying "a large quantity" of mothballs at a Walmart the day before they first appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

Upon examining his phone, investigators found "incriminating" text messages between him and fellow business owner Monroe discussing their objections to the native fowl.

Text conversations revealed plans for placement of the mothballs on the beach, officials said. That's what led investigators to Monroe as a suspect.

The men discussed how they "were going to do something" to prevent the birds from nesting on the beach, FWC officials said.

Black skimmers don't nest in trees. They kick beach sand to make depressions on the ground. Then they lay their eggs and raise their young near the surf.

"They're the worst birds," one of the men allegedly wrote in anticipation of nesting season.

"The bird people will put up fence around the area, and then the beach people will not be able to get to and from because they will fence around that space."

Cellphone tower data showed Monroe's phone was at the same location as Czyszczon's phone on both nights when the mothballs appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

The men feared that nests on the beach would lead to fewer customers and less money being spent there, authorities said.

"Why didn't you tell me we lose $25,000 to $50,000?" one allegedly wrote in a text.

Monroe and Czyszczon were charged with illegal dumping, a third-degree felony, according to Pinellas County court records. They also were charged with the "attempted take of a state-listed imperiled species by harassment," a misdemeanor, according to FWC officials.

About 6,800 black skimmers live in Florida. FWC officials estimate that several hundred live on the beaches of Pinellas County.

The pesticide in mothballs can harm people and wildlife that come into contact with their vapors, according to an educational publication by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS).

"With any pesticide, the label is the law," Brett W. Bultemeier, director of the UF/IFAS Pesticide Information Office, wrote in a 2021 educational publication about mothballs. "The label language is not simply a set of directions. Rather, they are requirements that are legally enforceable."

The birds probably weren't hurt by the "harassment," FWC officials said.

But it did delay their nesting, they said. That pushes the date that their young can fledge from the nest further back in the season. And that could put them in danger.

A big storm at the end of hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30, "can wipe out a colony if those young birds haven't fledged yet," an FWC official said.

title: Opinion - Are Republicans blind to the canaries in the Florida and Texas coal mines?
description: Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership.
fullText:
I have never understood how self-proclaimed or anointed election experts, who are wrong time and again, remain the go-to experts for much of the media. What I do understand is why they are wrong so often.

Many of these experts live in bubbles quite removed from Main Street America and especially the working-class voting population.

To be sure, Republicans have more than their fair share of the snobbish, pompous and the ignorant, living happily and hedonistically within those same bubbles of luxury that will never be attainable to many of their fellow Americans.

Having grown up in poverty myself, I can say that most in the working-class do not resent others' success.  They just want those who do attain or are handed that success to understand and address the plight of the disenfranchised and the powerless if they ever do find themselves in positions of power.

In my time, I have known many paycheck-to-paycheck parents and voters, many of whom still deeply believe in President Trump. And yet all say their paychecks buy less and less with each passing month.

My wife and I have done all right in life. But of late, every single time she comes back from the grocery chain store with just two small bags of items, she points out the ever-increasing prices.  This is no one's imagination. This is reality.

Some in the administration will claim until the cows come home that the stock market is doing great; 401(k) accounts are growing; and all of our rich friends are getting richer. But one truth for one class does not cancel out the quality-of-life crushing truth for another.

Politics, like much of life, is cyclical.  Democrats used to be really good at addressing bread and butter issues. Then Republicans cleverly hijacked that winning formula. And now, it seems to be swinging back toward the Democrats.

As we rapidly approach the midterms in November and the 2028 presidential election, history and reality are working against the Republicans. History reminds us that in 20 of the last 22 midterm elections, the party not occupying the Oval Office gained ground. That, coupled with the reality of more and more working class Americans struggling economically, should be a five-alarm warning for Republicans.

Yet, so many seem blissfully oblivious to it all.

As an example, I offer up the red states of Florida and Texas. Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership, but I well-connected Republicans in those two states are increasingly worried about the Senate race in Texas and the governor's race in Florida.

Aside from their concerns that the Republican Party is coming down on the wrong side of bread and butter issues, they worry that they are putting up flawed candidates in a midterm that already favors Democrats.

In Texas, a new Fox News poll shows Democratic senate candidate James Talarico (D) leading Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 3 points. And among "extremely motivated voters" from both parties, Talarico's advantage in the race grows to 6 points. Even worse, one-quarter of non-MAGA Republicans support Talarico. All this in a state Trump won by 14 points in 2024.

Why? One reason is that Republicans are wasting time and money attacking Talarico's personal life. Another is Ken Paxton's personal flaws. A third is that working-class Texas feels shunned by Republicans promoting what is supposed to be a great economy based on 401(k) performances.

A similar situation exists in Florida. Every Republican I speak to in that state believes term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) to be "the best governor in the nation." Many also believed that his wife Casey would have been a lock to replace him, but we will never know. President Trump, as is his prerogative, endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) before the Republican primary for governor had even begun. The primary is still coming up, but Donalds will be the Republican nominee.

In the meantime, he is getting pounded by negative attack ads that will be used against him by the eventual Democratic nominee (most likely former Republican Congressman David Jolly, now a Democrat) this fall. Florida Republicans I know are nervous.

That, once again, comes on top of real economic pain felt by every paycheck-to-paycheck voter.  Karl Rove, who driving force behind George W. Bush election as president, has warned that "Republicans risk making the same political mistake he believes cost Democrats the 2024 election, arguing the party is relying too heavily on favorable gross domestic product and job figures while failing to address the economic pressures many voters still feel.

Even as Democratic Socialists of America gain ground with outright communists winning nominations, a multitude of "canary in the coal mine" examples exist on the Republican side as well, including in Florida and Texas. If both of these flawed canddates fail, the Republican Party is in deep trouble.

I am no expert, but if I were the Republican leadership, I might be trying to figure out how to get some emergency oxygen to these canaries before it is too late.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

title: Why Florida dropped in ESPN's team recruiting rankings

fullText:
Florida football dropped one spot to No. 8 in the 2027 ESPN team recruiting rankings on Thursday.

The movement is a result of Miami landing No. 25 overall recruit and top-ranked athlete A'Mir Sears. The Hurricanes jumped three spots from No. 8 to No. 5, pushing the Gators, Oklahoma Sooners (No. 6) and Ohio State Buckeyes (No. 7) down one spot each.

Almost every other team in the top 10 stayed put, with Texas A&M and Notre Dame at the top of the list. Oregon and Texas flipped spots to Nos. 3 and 4, respectively, while Auburn and Texas Tech held steady at Nos. 9 and 10.

There isn't a ton of room for further movement over the next few months. All but four of the recruits ranked on the ESPN 300 are committed. Florida only has an offer to one of them: four-star running back Caden Waye out of Ola High School in McDonough, Georgia.

Waye included Florida in his top 12 back in December, but interest in him has dropped for several national programs. His only official visit of the summer was to UCF, and his list now includes Texas State, UTEP, Louisiana Tech and Missouri State.

He may no longer be a take for the Gators with four-star running back Andrew Beard committed from the class. Still, adding him to the commitment list could improve Florida's standing on ESPN's ranking moving forward.

fullText:
Florida State transfer forward Chauncey Wiggins has committed to Gonzaga, according to On3's Joe Tipton. He played the 2026 season at FSU after transferring from Clemson, but entered the transfer portal this cycle.

Wiggins was a player to watch for a potential fifth year of eligibility, On3 previously reported. A Colorado judge granted a class-wide preliminary injunction last week, which declared the Class of 2022 eligible for the 2026 season pending an NCAA appeal, opened the door for him to possibly return to college basketball.

The judge's order stated players who were returning could only play for their previous team, meaning they could not enter the portal outside of the window. However, Wiggins hit the open market in April after one season at FSU.

Chauncey Wiggins appeared in 32 games for Florida State last season, including 30 starts. He averaged a career-high 13.3 points while adding 3.9 rebounds per game, as well. That came after three seasons at Clemson, where he took on a starting role in 2024-25 when he started 26 out of 34 games played. That season, Wiggins averaged 8.3 points and 2.9 rebounds.

Judge Charlotte Sweeney's order came after the NCAA announced the implementation of its 5-year, age-based eligibility rule. Under the new guidelines, athletes will have a five-year eligibility clock beginning with their 19th birthday or when they enroll in college, whichever occurs sooner. However, athletes from the Class of 2022 – which just completed their fourth seasons – would not be "grandfathered" in under the new rules.

As a result, the NCAA faced multiple lawsuits, and Sweeney's ruling was for the entire class. However, she later clarified her ruling and said the transfer rules would not enjoined, meaning those athletes could not enter the portal. Additionally, roster limits in place under the House v. NCAA settlement also remain in effect, meaning schools cannot go beyond that figure if athletes decide to come back.

"The Court's order does not enjoin the operation of transfer rules," Sweeney wrote in the order, issued Aug. 2. "As the plain language of the preliminary injunction order and this order make clear, the Court's injunction concerns only the implementation of the Rule (as defined in the preliminary injunction order) and any Bylaw that prohibits Plaintiffs and Class Members from competing in a fifth season of collegiate athletics."

While a major decision, Sweeney's ruling is not necessarily final. The NCAA, as expected, is appealing it and hoping for a stay of the injunction. The governing body also issued a clarification which stated any athlete who signed a pro contract will not be eligible under terms of the judge's order.

fullText:
STARKVILLE – Zach Arnett hasn’t taken the podium at Mississippi State in a while.

The last time he did was in November 2023, back when he was in Year 1 as the team’s head coach. He was fired that month after going 4-6 leading up to that point, then bounced around for the next few years, taking assistant jobs at Ole Miss and Florida State.

On Monday morning, Arnett was back at that same podium, this time as MSU's defensive coordinator, a position he held from 2020-2022 before being named the head coach.

“I’m very thankful for the opportunity,” Arnett said. “Coach (Jeff) Lebby, he's got a great staff here, he runs a great program. I’m excited for the opportunity to be a part of it. Obviously, we’ve got to do our job and get some results on defense.”

MSU’s defense usually ranked in the top half of the SEC in points per game, yards per game and sacks with Arnett at the helm. Since then, the unit has ranked at or near the bottom of the conference in all three categories.

When Arnett first came back to Starkville, he saw a collection of players who checked a lot of boxes. Some can run, some can cover and some can win at the point of attack and beat blocks up front.

“That's ultimately all you can ask for as a coach,” Arnett said. “You feel like you got a talented room that has fun pieces to play around with. Now it's our job to put them in the right places. Like they say, you’ve got to get the right people on the bus, and you’ve got to get them in the right seats. So that's our job as coaches.”

Since replacing Arnett, Lebby has placed a strong emphasis on the culture “within the walls” of the football facility. When State’s new defensive coordinator sees film of this group, he sees players who are always excited to play and get after people.

Arnett will obviously work to instill his schematics and more when training camp starts on Thursday and in the weeks to follow leading up to the season opener, but he believes the most important building block is already in place.

“If you don't play with effort, no matter what you're doing schematically on either side of the ball, it's not going to be the difference-maker,” Arnett said. “Effort, physicality and execution. That's our job as coaches: to make sure we get that implemented by the time we get out of training camp and get into the season.”
